entries.question: AutoBoxing & AutoUnboxing
entries.answer:
- Introduced in Java 5 to support Collections & Generics.
- **Autoboxing**: Automatic conversion between **primitive → wrapper**
- **Unboxing**: Automatic conversion between **wrapper → primitive**

```java
Integer a = 10;   // Autoboxing (int → Integer)
int b = a;        // Unboxing (Integer → int)

/* What actually happens (compiler level) */
Integer a = Integer.valueOf(10);
int b = a.intValue();
```

1️⃣ **Byte Conversion in Java**

This is called **WIDENING PRIMITIVE CONVERSION**

🧠 **Basic Rule (Must Remember)**

Java follows this **fixed widening order**:

```
byte  → short → int → long → float → double
char  → int   → long → float → double
```

- Conversion is **implicit**
- **No cast required**
- **No compile-time error**

✔ Example 1:

```java
byte b = 10;

int i = b;       // byte → int (widening)
float f = i;     // int → float
double d = f;    // float → double

System.out.println(d); // 10.0
```

✔ Example 2: Valid char Widening:

```java
char c = 'A';   // Unicode 65

int i = c;      // 65
long l = c;
float f = c;
double d = c;
```

❌ Invalid Conversions

```java
byte b = c;     // ❌ compile-time error
short s = c;    // ❌ compile-time error
```

✔ Example 3: Direct Conversion (Chain Happens Internally)

```java
byte b = 10;
double d = b;  // byte → double directly (any step along the chain is allowed)
```

> ⚠️ Widening never needs a cast, but `int → float` and `long → float/double` can **lose precision** for very large numbers (`float` keeps only ~7 digits).

byte - 8 bits → `-128` to `127`
short - 16 bits → `-32,768` to `32,767`
char - 16 bits → `0` to `65,535`
int - 32 bits → `-2,147,483,648` to `2,147,483,647`
long - 64 bits `-9,223,372,036,854,775,808` to `9,223,372,036,854,775,807`
float - 32-bit floating point
double - 64-bit floating point

✔ Example 4: Widening vs Autoboxing (Very Important — a classic trap)

Java will **widen** OR **box**, but it will **not widen and then box** in one step:

```java
byte b = 10;

Integer i = b;  // ❌ compile error: byte cannot be converted to Integer
Long l = b;     // ❌ compile error: byte cannot be converted to Long

int n = b;      // ✅ widening only
Integer i2 = n; // ✅ boxing only
Object o = b;   // ✅ boxing to Byte, then Byte is an Object (o.getClass() → Byte)
```

✔ Example 5: Narrowing

```java
double d = 10.8;
int i = (int) d;     // 10  (fraction lost)

int x = 130;
byte b = (byte) x;  // -126 (overflow)
```

entries.question: JVM Internal Question
entries.answer:
```java
Integer x = 100;
Integer y = 100;
System.out.println(x == y); // true (cached)

Integer p = 200;
Integer q = 200;
System.out.println(p == q); // false (new objects)
```

👉 **Rule**:

- `==` compares **references**
- `.equals()` compares **values**
- JVM caches Integer objects in the range: `-128` to `127`

Runtime behavior:

```java
x --> cached Integer(100)
y --> cached Integer(100)
```

✔ Same object reference

```java
System.out.println(x == y); // true
```

🔹 **Real Production Bug**

```java
Integer count = null;
int total = count; // NullPointerException (auto-unboxing)
```

💥 **Why?**

- JVM tries: `count.intValue()` causing **NullPointerException**

🔹 **Performance Impact**

```java
Long sum = 0L;
for (long i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) {
     sum += i; // boxing + unboxing every iteration
}
```

⚠️ **Hidden cost** → creates unnecessary objects → GC pressure

✅ Better:

```java
long sum = 0L;
```

entries.question: How does HashMap work internally?
entries.answer:
A `HashMap` is an **array of buckets**. The key's hash decides the bucket, so `get` and `put` are **O(1)** on average. ![A hash function turns each key into a bucket index](../../../knowledge/visual-notes/under-the-hood/hash-table.svg) _Image: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hash_table_3_1_1_0_1_0_0_SP.svg) · Jorge Stolfi · CC BY-SA 3.0_ **`put(key, value)` step by step:** 1. `key.hashCode()` → spread the bits (`h ^ (h >>> 16)`). 2. Bucket index = `hash & (capacity - 1)` (capacity is a power of 2, default **16**). 3. Empty bucket → store the entry. 4. Same bucket already used (**collision**) → walk the entries; if `equals()` finds the same key, **replace** the value, else **add** a node. 5. A bucket with **more than 8** entries (and table ≥ 64) becomes a **red-black tree** → worst case O(log n) instead of O(n). 6. When size > capacity × **0.75** (load factor), the table **doubles** and entries are redistributed (**rehashing**). ```mermaid flowchart TD K["put(key, value)"] --> H["hash(key)"] --> I["index = hash & (n-1)"] I --> E{Bucket empty?} E -- yes --> N[Store entry] E -- no --> Q{"equals() matches a key?"} Q -- yes --> R[Replace value] Q -- no --> L["Add to list
(tree if more than 8)"] ```
entries.summary: A HashMap is an array of buckets. The key's hash decides the bucket, so get and put are O(1) on average.

(tree if more than 8)"]

entries.question: How do generics work in Java — wildcards, type erasure and PECS?
entries.answer:
**Generics** let one class or method work with many types **with compile-time checks**: `List<String>` can't accidentally hold an `Integer`.

```java
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items) {   // bounded type parameter
  T best = items.get(0);
  for (T item : items) if (item.compareTo(best) > 0) best = item;
  return best;
}
```

**Wildcards:**

| Wildcard | Means | You can |
|---|---|---|
| `List<?>` | a list of something | read as `Object` |
| `List<? extends Number>` | Number or a subtype | **read** Numbers (producer) |
| `List<? super Integer>` | Integer or a supertype | **add** Integers (consumer) |

**PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super:**

```java
static double sum(List<? extends Number> nums) { … }           // reads → extends
static void fill(List<? super Integer> out) { out.add(42); }    // writes → super
// Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)
```

**Type erasure:** generic types exist **only at compile time**. At runtime `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`. So you **can't**:
- `new T()` or `new T[10]`
- `if (obj instanceof List<String>)`
- overload `m(List<String>)` and `m(List<Integer>)`

entries.question: What garbage collectors does the JVM have, and how do they work?
entries.answer:
The GC frees objects that are no longer **reachable** from roots (thread stacks, static fields).

![The JVM: class loader, runtime data areas (heap, stacks, method area) and execution engine with the garbage collector](../../../knowledge/visual-notes/interview/jvm-architecture.png)

_Image: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:JvmSpec7.png) · Michelle Ridomi · CC BY-SA 4.0_

**Generational idea:** most objects die young.
- **Young generation** (Eden + 2 Survivor spaces) — new objects; cleaned often and fast (**minor GC**).
- **Old generation** — objects that survived several minor GCs; cleaned less often (**major/full GC**).

| Collector | Best for | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Serial** | tiny apps, single CPU | one thread, stops the app |
| **Parallel** | batch jobs, max throughput | many threads, still pauses |
| **G1** (default since Java 9) | most servers | splits heap into regions, aims for a pause target (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`) |
| **ZGC** | large heaps, low latency | pauses under ~1 ms, mostly concurrent; generational since Java 21 |
| **Shenandoah** | low latency | concurrent compaction |

**Stop-the-world pause** = all app threads stop while the GC works. Modern collectors keep these very short.

```bash
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g -XX:+UseZGC -Xlog:gc -jar app.jar
```

entries.question: What is the Java Memory Model and the "happens-before" rule?
entries.answer:
Each CPU core has caches, and the compiler/CPU may **reorder** instructions. So one thread's write isn't automatically **visible** to another thread. The **Java Memory Model (JMM)** defines when a write **is guaranteed** to be seen: when it **happens-before** the read.

**Main happens-before rules:**
1. **Program order** — inside one thread, earlier statements happen-before later ones.
2. **Monitor lock** — unlocking a lock happens-before the next lock of the same lock (`synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`).
3. **`volatile`** — a write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of it.
4. **Thread start** — `thread.start()` happens-before anything in that thread.
5. **Thread join** — everything in a thread happens-before `join()` returns.
6. **Transitivity** — A → B and B → C means A → C.

```java
class Task {
  private int result;
  private volatile boolean done;           // the volatile write "publishes" result too

  void finish() { result = 42; done = true; }                     // thread A
  void check() { if (done) System.out.println(result); }          // thread B: always 42
}
```

Without `volatile`, thread B might **never** see `done = true`, or see it but read an old `result`.
entries.summary: Each CPU core has caches, and the compiler/CPU may reorder instructions. So one thread's write isn't automatically visible to another thread. The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines when a write is guaranteed to be seen: when it happens-before the read.

entries.answer: ↪ No. It guarantees visibility, not atomicity — `count++` is read, add, write. Use `AtomicInteger` or a lock.

entries.question: Fixed Thread Pool vs Cached Thread Pool
entries.answer:
**Fixed Thread Pool**

- Fixed number of threads.
- Threads are **reused**.
- Good for **controlled workload**.

```java
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
```

✔ Predictable
✔ Prevents overload
❌ Tasks may wait

**Cached Thread Pool**

- Creates new threads **as needed**.
- Reuses idle threads.
- Good for **short-lived, fast tasks**.

```java
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
```

✔ Fast execution
❌ Can create too many threads (risk!)

**Comparison Table**

| Feature      | Fixed Thread Pool  | Cached Thread Pool |
| ------------ | ------------------ | ------------------ |
| Thread count | Fixed              | Unlimited          |
| Performance  | Stable             | Very fast          |
| Risk         | Low                | High (OOM)         |
| Use case     | Long-running tasks | Short tasks        |

entries.question: What does Serializable mean?
entries.answer:
**`Serializable`** is a **marker interface** that is used to **convert Java Object into a byte stream**.

Serializable is like a tag you put on a class to tell Java:

> Hey JVM, this object is allowed to be converted into bytes.

Because Java asks:

> Are you sure you want this object to leave memory?

Serialization is commonly used for:

- Saving objects to a **file**
- Sending objects over a **network**
- Caching objects (Redis, session storage)
- Passing objects between JVMs

🔹 **Marker Interface**

A marker interface is an **interface with no methods** that tells the JVM to treat a class differently.

```java
// Marker interface: no methods, it just "tags" the class
public interface Serializable { }

class User implements Serializable {}

// The code that needs the tag checks it with instanceof:
// ObjectOutputStream throws NotSerializableException if !(obj instanceof Serializable)
```

> **Before annotations (Java 5), marker interfaces were the only way to tag a class.** Today annotations (e.g. `@FunctionalInterface`, `@Entity`) are often used instead — but a marker interface also gives you a **type** the compiler can check.

| Marker Interface                   | Purpose                     |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `Serializable`                     | Allows object serialization |
| `Cloneable`                        | Allows object cloning       |
| `RandomAccess`                     | Optimizes list access       |
| `SingleThreadModel` _(deprecated)_ | Thread safety hint          |

```java
// Write an object to a file, then read it back
try (var out = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("user.bin"))) {
    out.writeObject(new User(1, "Asha"));
}
try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("user.bin"))) {
    User copy = (User) in.readObject();
}
```

🔹 `serialVersionUID`

```java
private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
```

- Ensures **version compatibility**
- Prevents `InvalidClassException`

❌ Without it:

Java secretly creates its own version number based on: `fields`, `types`, `structure`.  
Now you change the class (even slightly), Java creates a different version number.  
Later, when deserializing, Java compares: **version in saved data** and **version of current class**

```text
InvalidClassException: local class incompatible
```

🔹 `transient` Keyword

Used to **exclude fields from serialization**.

```java
class User implements Serializable {
    int id;
    transient String password;
}
```

- `password` will **NOT** be serialized
- After deserialization → `password = null`

🔹 `transient` vs `@Transient`

**transient** is a Java keyword that excludes a field from **serialization**
**@Transient** excludes a field from **database persistence**

🔹 Serializable vs Externalizable

| Feature     | Serializable | Externalizable                  |
| ----------- | ------------ | ------------------------------- |
| Methods     | None         | `writeExternal`, `readExternal` |
| Control     | Automatic    | Full control                    |
| Complexity  | Simple       | Complex                         |
| Performance | Slower       | Faster (custom)                 |

- **Caching** — some caches store objects with Java serialization by default.

```

> ⚠️ For **messages** (Kafka, RabbitMQ) and **APIs**, use JSON, Avro or Protobuf instead — not Java serialization.

entries.question: Serializable vs JSON
entries.answer:
| Serializable                      | JSON                        |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Java-specific                     | Language-independent        |
| Binary (bytes)                    | Text (readable)             |
| JVM handles it                    | Library handles it (Jackson) |
| Not necessarily smaller or faster (stores class metadata) | Simple and fast enough for most uses |

entries.question: Explain JVM memory structure. Heap vs Stack vs Metaspace
entries.answer:
| Area           | What Lives Here               |
| -------------- | ----------------------------- |
| **Stack**      | Local variables, method calls |
| **Heap**       | Objects, arrays               |
| **Metaspace**  | Class metadata                |
| **Code Cache** | JIT compiled code             |

```java
public class MemoryDemo { // Metaspace (class metadata: methods, field layout)

    static int staticCount = 100; // Heap (static fields live with the Class object on the heap since Java 8)

    public static void main(String[] args) { // Stack (method call)

        int localPrimitive = 10;      // Stack (local primitive)
        Object localReference;        // Stack (reference variable)

        Object obj = new Object();    // Heap (object)
        int[] numbers = new int[5];   // Heap (array)
        String str = new String("Hi");// Heap (object)

        localReference = str;         // Stack -> Heap reference

        demoMethod(obj);              // Stack (method call)
    }

    static void demoMethod(Object param) { // Stack (new stack frame)

        Object localObj;              // Stack (local reference)
        localObj = new Object();      // Heap (object)

        int x = 5;                    // Stack (local primitive)
    }
}

```

entries.question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions – what is your strategy?
entries.answer:
**The difference:** the compiler **forces** you to handle or declare a **checked** exception; it doesn't for an **unchecked** one. Both happen at runtime.

| Checked | Unchecked |
|---|---|
| Extends `Exception` (not `RuntimeException`) | Extends `RuntimeException` |
| Must `catch` it or declare `throws` | No compiler check |
| `IOException`, `SQLException`, `ClassNotFoundException` | `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `ArithmeticException` |
| For problems a caller can **reasonably recover** from | For **programming errors** and business rule violations |

```java
void readFile() throws IOException { ... }        // checked: callers must deal with it

void setAge(int age) {
    if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age must be >= 0");   // unchecked
}
```

**Strategy in a Spring app:**

- Use **unchecked custom exceptions** for business errors (`OrderNotFoundException`) — they don't clutter every method signature, and a global handler turns them into HTTP responses.
- **Wrap checked exceptions** from libraries at the boundary into unchecked ones, keeping the cause.
- Catch an exception only where you can **do something** (retry, fallback, add context) — never catch and ignore.
entries.summary: The difference: the compiler forces you to handle or declare a checked exception; it doesn't for an unchecked one. Both happen at runtime.

entries.question: Why does `@Transactional` matter here?
entries.answer: ↪ By default Spring rolls back only on **unchecked** exceptions. A checked exception commits the transaction unless you set `rollbackFor = Exception.class`.

entries.question: How do you implement global HTTP status handling in Spring Boot without setting the status code in each controller method?

Three options, from most to least common: 1. **`@RestControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler`** — one class maps each exception to a status (see above). 2. **`@ResponseStatus` on the exception class** — simplest for fixed cases: ```java @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) public class UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException { ... } ``` 3. **`ResponseStatusException`** — throw a status directly in rare one-off cases: ```java throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Email already used"); ``` Controllers then just return the happy-path result; errors are handled centrally. ```mermaid flowchart LR C[Controller] -- "throws UserNotFoundException" --> A["@RestControllerAdvice"] A --> H["@ExceptionHandler
maps exception → status"] H --> R["404 + JSON error body"] ```

entries.question: If I replace GET with PUT, can I still fetch records?
entries.answer:
Technically **yes** — the method just returns data. But it's **wrong for REST**:

- `GET` is **safe** (changes nothing) and **cacheable**; browsers, CDNs and proxies rely on that.
- `PUT` means "**replace** this resource" — clients, caches and API tools treat it as a write.

Using PUT to read loses caching, confuses API consumers and documentation (OpenAPI), and may trigger CSRF protection meant for writes. Use the method that matches the action.

entries.question: Can we get Request Body in GET?
entries.answer:
**Avoid it.** The HTTP spec (RFC 9110) says a body on GET has **no defined meaning**, so different tools treat it differently:

- Browsers' `fetch()` / `XMLHttpRequest` **can't send** a GET body at all.
- Some proxies, CDNs and HTTP clients **drop** it; caches ignore it (so results may be cached wrongly).
- Spring MVC will actually bind `@RequestBody` on a GET **if a body arrives**, but if it's missing you get `HttpMessageNotReadableException: Required request body is missing`.

✅ **Use query parameters** for filters:

```java
@GetMapping("/users")
public List<User> search(@RequestParam String name, @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page) { ... }
```

For very complex searches, use `POST /users/search` with a JSON body.

entries.question: What makes an API RESTful?
entries.answer:
REST is an architectural style where everything is a **resource** with a URL, and standard HTTP methods say what to do with it. Key ideas:

- **Resources, not actions:** `/orders/42`, not `/getOrder?id=42`.
- **Standard methods:** GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes.
- **Stateless:** each request carries everything needed (e.g. a token); the server keeps no session between calls, so any server can handle it.
- **Standard status codes and representations** (usually JSON), and cacheable responses where possible.

**Example:** `GET /customers/7/orders?status=PAID` → `200 OK` with a JSON list.

entries.question: What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST? Which are idempotent?
entries.answer:
| Method | Meaning | Idempotent? | Safe (read-only)? |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | Read | Yes | Yes |
| POST | Create / trigger an action | **No** | No |
| PUT | Replace the whole resource | Yes | No |
| PATCH | Change some fields | Not guaranteed | No |
| DELETE | Remove | Yes | No |

**Idempotent** = sending the same request twice leaves the same result as once — safe to retry after a timeout. To make POST retry-safe (e.g. payments), accept an **`Idempotency-Key`** header and return the first result for repeats.

entries.question: How do you name REST endpoints well?
entries.answer:
- Plural nouns for collections: `/orders`, `/orders/{id}`.
- Nest only for clear ownership, one level deep: `/customers/{id}/orders`.
- Lowercase with hyphens: `/payment-methods`.
- Filters, sorting and paging as query parameters: `/orders?status=PAID&sort=-createdAt&page=2`.
- Actions that don't fit CRUD become sub-resources: `POST /orders/{id}/cancel`.

entries.question: How do you paginate large lists?
entries.answer:
| Style | Request | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Offset** | `?page=3&size=20` | Simple, can jump to any page | Slow on deep pages; items shift when data changes |
| **Cursor (keyset)** | `?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&limit=20` | Fast at any depth, stable | Only next/previous, no page numbers |

Return metadata so clients know what's next:

```json
{ "items": [], "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6MTIwfQ", "hasMore": true }
```

Use cursor pagination for feeds and big tables; offset is fine for small admin lists. Always cap the page size.

entries.question: How do you version a REST API?
entries.answer:
Version only for **breaking changes** (removing or renaming fields, changing meaning). Adding optional fields is not breaking.

- **URL path:** `/api/v1/orders` — the most common, and the easiest to see and route.
- **Header:** `Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json` or a custom header — cleaner URLs, harder to test.
- Run old and new versions side by side, announce a deprecation date (`Deprecation` / `Sunset` headers), and watch traffic before removing the old one.
entries.summary: Version only for breaking changes (removing or renaming fields, changing meaning). Adding optional fields is not breaking.

entries.question: What should an API error response look like?
entries.answer:
A consistent JSON body with the right status code. A common standard is **Problem Details** (RFC 9457, `application/problem+json`):

```json
{
  "type": "https://api.shop.com/errors/insufficient-stock",
  "title": "Insufficient stock",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Only 2 units of SKU-881 are left.",
  "instance": "/orders/A1043"
}
```

- 400 bad input (list which fields), 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 validation failed, 429 too many requests, 500 server error.
- Never expose stack traces or SQL errors to clients. Spring Boot 3 supports Problem Details through `ProblemDetail`.

entries.question: How do you cache REST responses?
entries.answer:
- **`Cache-Control`** tells clients and CDNs how long to keep a response: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300`.
- **`ETag`** + **`If-None-Match`**: the client sends the version it has; if nothing changed, the server replies **304 Not Modified** with no body, saving bandwidth.
- Cache only safe GETs; never cache personal data publicly (use `private` or `no-store`).

**Example:** a product catalogue cached at the CDN for 5 minutes takes most of the load off the database during a sale.

entries.question: How do you secure a REST API?
entries.answer:
- **HTTPS only.**
- **Authentication:** OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect with short-lived JWT access tokens for users; API keys or client credentials for server-to-server calls.
- **Authorization on every endpoint** — check the caller owns the resource (prevents IDOR).
- **Validate input** and limit request size; use parameterised queries.
- **Rate limiting** per client (return 429 with `Retry-After`).
- Don't put secrets or tokens in URLs (they end up in logs); allow CORS only for known origins.

See also: [Web application security (OWASP)](../../security/01-Web-Security-OWASP.md)

entries.question: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC — when would you use each?
entries.answer:
| | REST | GraphQL | gRPC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shape | Many URLs, fixed responses | One endpoint, client chooses fields | Methods from a `.proto` contract |
| Format | JSON over HTTP | JSON over HTTP | Binary (Protocol Buffers) over HTTP/2 |
| Best for | Public APIs, simple CRUD, caching | Many UIs needing different data shapes | Fast service-to-service calls, streaming |
| Watch out | Over- or under-fetching | Caching, query cost limits | Browsers need a proxy; harder to debug by hand |

Many systems use **REST outside, gRPC inside**.
entries.summary: Many systems use REST outside, gRPC inside.

entries.question: What is Spring, Why it was introduced?
entries.answer:
Spring is a **lightweight, modular, inversion-of-control (IoC) based framework** that helps build loosely coupled, testable, enterprise Java applications.

**Core Principles**

- Inversion of Control (IoC)
  - Dependency Injection (DI)
  - Spring IoC Container
- Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP)
- Declarative Transactions
- Modular Design

entries.question: Common Spring Dependency Injection Errors – Why Do They Happen?
entries.answer:
Almost every injection error means Spring **can't find exactly one bean** of the type you asked for, or you're using an object **Spring didn't create**:

| Error | Usual cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` | Class isn't a bean (no `@Component`/`@Service`), or outside the scanned packages | Add a stereotype annotation; keep it under the `@SpringBootApplication` package |
| `NullPointerException` on a dependency | Object created with `new`, or field injection not done | Let Spring create it; use constructor injection |
| `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` | Two beans of the same type | `@Primary` or `@Qualifier("name")` |
| `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` | Circular dependency A → B → A | Redesign; extract a third class |

Details for each case follow.

entries.question: Can you explain the different bean scopes in Spring?
entries.answer:
Spring controls **how many instances** of a bean exist.

| Scope         | Description                          |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `singleton`   | One instance per container (default) |
| `prototype`   | New instance every request           |
| `request`     | One per HTTP request                 |
| `session`     | One per HTTP session                 |
| `application` | One per ServletContext               |

```java
@Scope("prototype")
@Component
public class ReportGenerator {}
```

entries.question: Explain the lifecycle of a Spring bean and how you can intervene at different stages of its initialization and destruction.
entries.answer:
**Bean lifecycle at a glance** (where you can step in is in brackets): ```mermaid flowchart TD A[1. Create object: constructor] --> B["2. Inject dependencies
(@Autowired fields / setters)"] B --> C["3. Aware callbacks
(BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware)"] C --> D["4. BeanPostProcessor: before init"] D --> E["5. Init
(@PostConstruct, afterPropertiesSet, initMethod)"] E --> F["6. BeanPostProcessor: after init
(proxies for @Transactional, AOP)"] F --> G[7. Bean ready to use] G --> H["8. Context closes: destroy
(@PreDestroy, destroy, destroyMethod)"] ``` The rest of this answer shows how Spring Boot gets to step 1: what happens from `main()` until beans are created. 🔹 JVM STARTS → `main()` METHOD ```java @SpringBootApplication // Combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan public class MyApplication { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args); } } ``` - JVM loads `MyApplication` - JVM calls `main()` - Control enters Spring Boot 🔹 `SpringApplication.run()` runs and create `SpringApplication` object ```java public static ConfigurableApplicationContext run( Class primarySource, String... args) ``` ```java public static ConfigurableApplicationContext run(Class primarySource, String... args) { return new SpringApplication(primarySource).run(args); } ``` - `run()` is static, only as an **entry point** - Inside: - `new SpringApplication(primarySource)` → **object is created** - That object’s **non-static `run()` method** is called ✔ Static method → creates instance → instance drives everything 🔹 Application Type Detection (Servlet vs Reactive) Inside the **SpringApplication constructor**, Spring checks the **classpath**, NOT annotations. | Found on classpath | Application Type | | ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | `jakarta.servlet.Servlet` (`javax.servlet` before Boot 3) | SERVLET (Spring MVC, Tomcat) | | `org.springframework.web.reactive.DispatcherHandler` | REACTIVE (WebFlux) | | None | NONE (CLI / Batch app) | This can be found in `pom.xml` **pom.xml** ```xml spring-boot-starter-web ``` Classpath contains: - jakarta.servlet.Servlet - Tomcat (default; Jetty can be swapped in) > ➡ Spring Boot chooses SERVLET 🔹 `run()` METHOD – High Level Flow Once the `SpringApplication` object exists, its **instance `run()`** method executes: 1. Prepare environment 2. Create ApplicationContext 3. Load configuration classes 4. Refresh context 5. Create beans 6. Start web server 🔹 Environment Preparation (ONLY properties loading) Spring loads configuration properties **before** creating the container. **Properties are loaded from many sources. Highest priority first — a higher one overrides a lower one:** 1. Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`) 2. JVM system properties (`-Dserver.port=9090`) 3. OS environment variables (`SERVER_PORT=9090`) 4. Profile-specific files: `application-{profile}.properties` / `.yml` 5. `application.properties` / `application.yml` 6. Defaults in code (`@PropertySource`, `SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties`) (Files **outside** the JAR, e.g. `./config/application.yml`, beat the same files packaged **inside** it.) > 💡 That's why the same JAR can run anywhere: production overrides a value with an environment variable instead of rebuilding. ✔ These values are stored ✔ Used later during bean creation ✔ No beans created here 🔹 ApplicationContext Creation After environment is ready, Spring creates the container. ```java // 1. Create a new ApplicationContext instance AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(); // 2. Register configuration classes or individual beans context.register(AppConfig.class) // Optional in Spring Boot ``` It creates an empty Spring ApplicationContext object that is capable of: - Accepting Java-based configuration (`@Configuration`, `@Component`) - Creating and managing a `BeanFactory` later - Starting the Spring lifecycle when `refresh()` is called > At this point, Spring has NOT started yet 🔹 `refresh()` is called (the real work starts) Spring now calls: ```java context.refresh(); ``` This is where **everything meaningful happens**. - Create the REAL Container ```java DefaultListableBeanFactory beanFactory = new DefaultListableBeanFactory(); ``` > ✅ THIS is the IoC container - Load Bean Definitions - `@SpringBootConfiguration` - `@ComponentScan` - `@EnableAutoConfiguration` 🔹 `@SpringBootConfiguration` or `@Configuration`? ```java @SpringBootConfiguration public class MyApplication {} // Is internally equivalent to: @Configuration public class MyApplication {} ``` - Parses the class - Finds `@Bean` methods - Registers **bean definitions** > ⚠️ No beans created yet 🔹 `@ComponentScan` **Find components in packages** - Scans packages - Registers bean definitions for: - `@Component` - `@Service` - `@Repository` - `@Controller` > ⚠️ Still no objects created 🔹 `@EnableAutoConfiguration` - Reads a list of auto-configuration classes from: ``` META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (Boot 2.7+) META-INF/spring.factories (Boot 2.x only — no longer read for auto-config in Boot 3) ``` - Loads **configuration classes** - Applies conditions: - Class present? - Property enabled? - Bean already exists? ✔ Registers **conditional bean definitions** Example: - If `DataSource` class exists → register datasource beans - If `spring.datasource.*` exists → enable DB auto config > ⚠️ Still no objects created 🔹 **Beans are created ONLY after all configuration and scanning is complete** **Trigger point** ```java preInstantiateSingletons() ``` - Create object (constructor) - Inject dependencies - Call `@PostConstruct` - Bean is ready

entries.answer:
⚠️ It depends on the bean **names**:

- **Different names, same type**: both are created, and injecting by type throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` unless you use `@Primary` or `@Qualifier`.

Best practice: make the profiles mutually exclusive (`@Profile("dev")` vs `@Profile("!dev")`).

entries.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator?
entries.answer:
**Spring Boot Actuator** is a production-ready feature of Spring Boot that helps you **monitor, manage, and inspect your application** while it is running.

> Actuator answers How is my application behaving right now?

| Endpoint             | Purpose                      |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `/actuator/health`   | Application health           |
| `/actuator/info`     | App metadata                 |
| `/actuator/metrics`  | JVM & custom metrics         |
| `/actuator/env`      | Environment properties       |
| `/actuator/beans`    | Spring beans                 |
| `/actuator/mappings` | Request mappings             |
| `/actuator/loggers`  | Change log levels at runtime |
| `/actuator/shutdown` | Graceful shutdown (optional) |

🔹 Step 1: Add Dependency

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

🔹 Step 2: Enable Endpoints

By default, only `/actuator/health` is exposed over HTTP (`/info` too before Spring Boot 2.5). Expose others explicitly — and protect sensitive ones like `env`, `beans` and `heapdump` with Spring Security.

```properties
# application.properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
```

entries.question: What is Spring AOP, Why it was introduced?
entries.summary: Spring AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) is a module of the Spring Framework that helps you separate cross-cutting concerns (like logging, security, transactions, monitoring) from your business logic.

entries.question: Can Spring AOP intercept private methods?
entries.answer:
No. Spring AOP works through **proxies**, so it only sees calls that go **through the proxy** to a public method (CGLIB proxies can also catch protected/package-visible ones).

Same trap as `@Transactional`: when one method calls another **in the same class** (`this.other()`), the call skips the proxy and no advice runs. Use AspectJ weaving if you really need private methods or self-calls.

entries.question: What is Spring Modular Design?
entries.answer:
![ModularDesign Image](/src/assets/backend/spring-modular-design.png)

**Spring Modular Design** means the Spring Framework is built as a collection of independent, loosely coupled modules, where each module solves a specific concern (core container, web, data access, security, etc.).

> 👉 You only include what you need, keeping applications lightweight, maintainable, and scalable.

| Types                                | Responsibilities                                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Spring Core Container**            | IoC Container, Bean lifecycle, Dependency Injection, Configuration Mgmt |
| **Spring Data Access / Integration** | JDBC, ORM (Hibernate, JPA), Transactions, Spring Data JPA               |
| **Spring Web Layer**                 | Spring MVC, Spring WebFlux (Reactive)                                   |
| **Spring Security**                  | Authentication, Authorization, CSRF protection, OAuth2, JWT             |
| **Spring AOP**                       | Logging, Security, Transactions, Auditing                               |

entries.question: application.properties vs application.yml?
entries.answer:
Both are used to **configure Spring Boot applications** (DB config, server port, logging, etc.).

| application.properties      | application.yml          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Key = value format          | YAML (indentation-based) |
| Easy for small configs      | Best for complex configs |
| Less readable for hierarchy | Very readable & clean    |
| No indentation              | Indentation is mandatory |

Spring Boot supports **both**, but **YAML is preferred** for large projects.

**Example**

application.properties

```properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/testdb
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=admin
```

application.yml

```yaml
server:
  port: 8081

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/testdb
    username: root
    password: admin
```

> prefer `application.yml` for readability when configs grow.

entries.question: Explain the Spring MVC request flow (DispatcherServlet).
entries.answer:
Every HTTP request goes through one **front controller**, the `DispatcherServlet`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant F as Filters (security, CORS)
  participant D as DispatcherServlet
  participant HM as HandlerMapping
  participant I as Interceptors
  participant Ctl as @RestController
  participant MC as HttpMessageConverter (Jackson)
  C->>F: GET /api/users/7
  F->>D: request
  D->>HM: which method handles this?
  HM-->>D: UserController.get(Long)
  D->>I: preHandle()
  D->>Ctl: get(7) — args resolved (@PathVariable, @RequestBody…)
  Ctl-->>D: UserDto
  D->>MC: convert to JSON
  D->>I: postHandle / afterCompletion
  D-->>C: 200 OK + JSON
```

1. **Filters** run first (servlet level — Spring Security lives here).
2. `DispatcherServlet` asks **HandlerMapping** which controller method matches the URL and HTTP method.
3. **Interceptors** `preHandle` run.
4. **Argument resolvers** build the parameters (`@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestBody` + validation).
5. The controller runs.
6. **Message converters** (Jackson) turn the return value into JSON.
7. Exceptions go to `@ExceptionHandler` / `@RestControllerAdvice`.

entries.question: What is Declarative Transactions, Spring Transactions & Spring Data JPA?
entries.answer:
1. Declarative Transactions (Concept)

A **style of transaction management**, not a framework.

- You **declare** transaction rules
- You do **not** write `begin / commit / rollback` code

Example:

```java
@Transactional
public void placeOrder() { }
```

> ✔ Focus on _what_ should be transactional
> ✔ Not _how_ it is implemented

2. Spring Transactions (Implementation)

Spring’s **transaction management framework** provided by the **Spring Framework**.

- Implements **Declarative Transactions**
- Uses **AOP + proxies**
- Manages commit / rollback automatically

Under the hood:

- `PlatformTransactionManager`
- Integrates with JDBC, JPA, Hibernate

Example:

```java
@Service
@Transactional
public class OrderService { }
```

> ✔ This is the **engine** that makes declarative transactions work

3. Spring Data JPA (Usage Layer)

A **data access abstraction** built on top of JPA + Spring Transactions.

- Auto-provides CRUD repositories
- Uses Spring Transactions internally
- Many repository methods are transactional by default

Example:

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {}
```

> ✔ You usually **don’t write transaction code**
> ✔ Spring Data JPA handles it for you

4. Transaction Propagation

- REQUIRED (Default – 90% use case)

  ```java
  @Transactional
  public void placeOrder() {
      paymentService.pay(); // joins same transaction
  }
  ```

  > ✔ If any method fails → everything rolls back

- REQUIRES_NEW
  - Suspends existing transaction
  - Starts a new independent transaction

  ```java
  @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
  public void logAudit() { }
  ```

- SUPPORTS
  - Uses transaction only if one exists
  - Otherwise runs without transaction

  ```java
  @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.SUPPORTS)
  public void readData() { }
  ```

  > ✔ Good for read-only operations

- NOT_SUPPORTED
  - Always runs without transaction

  ```java
  @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NOT_SUPPORTED)
  public void exportData() { }
  ```
entries.summary: Declarative Transactions (Concept)

codeBlocks.code:
@Transactional
public void placeOrder() { }
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {}

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
  public void logAudit() { }

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.SUPPORTS)
  public void readData() { }

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NOT_SUPPORTED)
  public void exportData() { }

entries.question: When Should You Use DTO?
entries.answer:
Use DTO when:

- You don’t want to expose entity directly
- You need **only selected fields**
- API response should be lightweight

🔹 Why we should NOT expose entity directly?

Exposing entity causes:

- ❌ Security risk (sensitive fields like `passwordHash` exposed)
- ❌ Lazy loading issues (`LazyInitializationException`, or N+1 queries while serializing)
- ❌ Tight coupling between DB & API — renaming a column breaks clients
- ❌ Accidental updates to DB fields (mass assignment)

```java
public record UserDto(Long id, String name, String email) {
    static UserDto from(User u) { return new UserDto(u.getId(), u.getName(), u.getEmail()); }
}
```
entries.summary: You don’t want to expose entity directly You need only selected fields API response should be lightweight

entries.question: What is the N+1 Problem? How to solve it?
entries.summary: When fetching a parent entity, Hibernate fires 1 query for parent + N queries for children.

entries.question: What happens in DB?
entries.answer:
```sql
1 query → fetch orders
N queries → fetch items for each order
```

❌ Performance killer

✅ Solutions

1. Fetch Join (Best & Most Used)

```java
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items")
List<Order> findAllWithItems();
```

2. EntityGraph

```java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
List<Order> findAll();
```

3. Batch Fetching — load children for many parents in one `IN (...)` query

```properties
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50
```

> ⚠️ `JOIN FETCH` on a collection **plus** `Pageable` makes Hibernate load everything and paginate **in memory** (warning HHH90003004). For paged lists, page the parents first, then use batch fetching or a second query for the children.

> _N+1 occurs due to lazy loading. I solve it using fetch joins or EntityGraph._
entries.summary: Performance killer

1 query → fetch orders
N queries → fetch items for each order

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
List<Order> findAll();

entries.question: Is @JoinColumn mandatory? If not, what happens if we don’t use it?
entries.answer:
**No.** Without it, JPA uses a default foreign-key column name: `<field name>_<referenced primary key>` — for `private Order order;` that's `order_id`.

```java
@ManyToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "order_ref", nullable = false)   // custom name + NOT NULL
private Order order;
```

Add `@JoinColumn` when the column name differs from the default (existing databases), or to set constraints:

It tells:

- Which column
- Nullable?
- Unique?
- FK constraint?
entries.summary: No. Without it, JPA uses a default foreign-key column name: _ — for private Order order; that's order_id.

entries.question: JPQL vs Native Query
entries.answer:
| Feature        | JPQL         | Native Query     |
| -------------- | ------------ | ---------------- |
| Works on       | Entity names | Table names      |
| DB Independent | ✅ Yes       | ❌ No            |
| Performance    | Good         | Sometimes faster |
| Portability    | High         | Low              |

**JPQL Example**

```java
@Query("SELECT e FROM Employee e WHERE e.salary > :salary")
List<Employee> findHighPaid(@Param("salary") double salary);
```

**Native Query Example**

```java
@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM employee WHERE salary > ?1", nativeQuery = true)   // ?1 = first parameter
List<Employee> findHighPaid(double salary);
```

- ✅ **JPQL** → 90% of cases
- ✅ **Native** → Complex joins, DB-specific features

> _JPQL is preferred for portability; native queries only when JPQL is insufficient._
entries.summary: Native Query Example

entries.question: First-Level vs Second-Level Cache
entries.answer:
**First-Level Cache**

- Enabled by default
- **Scope: Session / EntityManager**
- Cannot be turned off

```java
Employee e1 = em.find(Employee.class, 1);
Employee e2 = em.find(Employee.class, 1);
// DB hit happens only once
```

**Second-Level Cache**

- Optional
- **Shared across sessions**
- Requires configuration (Ehcache, Hazelcast)

```properties
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.region.factory_class=jcache   # plus a JCache provider such as Ehcache 3
```

```java
@Entity
@Cacheable                                         // opt this entity in
@org.hibernate.annotations.Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE)
public class Country { ... }
```

Good for data that is read often and changes rarely (countries, product categories).

**Comparison**

| Cache        | Scope       | Default |
| ------------ | ----------- | ------- |
| First-level  | Session     | ✅ Yes  |
| Second-level | Application | ❌ No   |

> _First-level cache is mandatory and session-scoped; second-level cache is optional and shared._
entries.summary: First-Level Cache

codeBlocks.code:
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.cache.region.factory_class=jcache   # plus a JCache provider such as Ehcache 3

entries.question: What are the Spring stereotype annotations (`@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`)?
entries.answer:
Stereotype annotations mark a class as a **Spring bean**, so component scanning finds it and Spring creates it. The specific ones also say which **layer** the class belongs to.

| Annotation    | Where It Is Used | Explanation                                          |
| ------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `@Component`  | Class level      | Marks a class as a Spring bean (generic stereotype). |
| `@Service`    | Class level      | Marks service/business logic class.                  |
| `@Repository` | Class level      | Marks DAO class; enables DB exception translation.   |
entries.summary: Stereotype annotations mark a class as a Spring bean, so component scanning finds it and Spring creates it. The specific ones also say which layer the class belongs to.

entries.question: Is there a functional difference between `@Component` and `@Service`?
entries.answer: ↪ No — `@Service` is a `@Component` with a clearer name. Only `@Repository` adds behaviour: it translates database exceptions into Spring's `DataAccessException`.
entries.summary: No — @Service is a @Component with a clearer name. Only @Repository adds behaviour: it translates database exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException.

entries.question: Which annotations are used for dependency injection in Spring?
entries.answer:
These annotations tell Spring **which bean to hand in** where. Prefer constructor injection; with a single constructor, `@Autowired` isn't even needed.

| Annotation   | Where It Is Used             | Explanation                                                                                         |
| ------------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@Autowired` | Field / Constructor / Setter | Injects dependency automatically by **type**.                                                       |
| `@Qualifier` | Field / Parameter            | Specifies which bean to inject when multiple beans of same type exist.                              |
| `@Primary`   | Class level (on bean)        | Marks a bean as the default choice when multiple candidates exist.                                  |
| `@Resource`  | Field / Setter               | Injects dependency by **name** (Java standard annotation).                                          |
| `@Inject`    | Field / Constructor / Setter | Similar to `@Autowired` (from JSR-330); injects by type.                                            |
| `@Lookup`    | Method level                 | Tells Spring to return a new bean instance dynamically (used for prototype beans inside singleton). |
entries.summary: These annotations tell Spring which bean to hand in where. Prefer constructor injection; with a single constructor, @Autowired isn't even needed.

entries.question: Two beans implement the same interface. How does Spring choose?
entries.answer: ↪ Mark one `@Primary` (the default), or name the one you want with `@Qualifier("beanName")` at the injection point.
entries.summary: Mark one @Primary (the default), or name the one you want with @Qualifier("beanName") at the injection point.

entries.question: Which annotations control a Spring bean's lifecycle and scope?
entries.answer:
Lifecycle annotations run your code **after a bean is created** and **before it is destroyed**; scope annotations decide **how many instances** exist.

| Annotation                   | Where It Is Used                   | Explanation                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@PostConstruct`             | Method level                       | Runs once after bean creation and dependency injection; used for initialization logic.       |
| `@PreDestroy`                | Method level                       | Runs before bean is destroyed; used for cleanup logic.                                       |
| `InitializingBean`           | Class level (implements interface) | Provides `afterPropertiesSet()` method for initialization (alternative to `@PostConstruct`). |
| `DisposableBean`             | Class level (implements interface) | Provides `destroy()` method for cleanup (alternative to `@PreDestroy`).                      |
| `@Bean(initMethod="...")`    | Method level                       | Specifies a custom initialization method for a bean.                                         |
| `@Bean(destroyMethod="...")` | Method level                       | Specifies a custom destroy method for a bean.                                                |
| `@Lazy`                      | Class / Method level               | Delays bean initialization until it is first requested.                                      |
| `BeanPostProcessor`          | Class level (implements interface) | Allows custom logic before and after bean initialization.                                    |
| `@Scope("singleton")`        | Class / `@Bean` method level       | Single shared instance for the entire application (default scope).                           |
| `@Scope("prototype")`        | Class / `@Bean` method level       | Creates a new bean instance every time it is requested.                                      |
| `@RequestScope`              | Class level                        | One bean instance per HTTP request (web applications only).                                  |
| `@SessionScope`              | Class level                        | One bean instance per HTTP session (per user session).                                       |
| `@ApplicationScope`          | Class level                        | One bean per ServletContext (shared across the whole web app).                               |
entries.summary: Lifecycle annotations run your code after a bean is created and before it is destroyed; scope annotations decide how many instances exist.

entries.question: Why might `@PreDestroy` not run on a prototype bean?
entries.answer: ↪ Spring creates prototype beans but doesn't manage them afterwards, so it never calls their destroy callbacks.
entries.summary: Spring creates prototype beans but doesn't manage them afterwards, so it never calls their destroy callbacks.

entries.question: Which annotations handle transactions and AOP in Spring?
entries.answer:
`@Transactional` wraps a method in a database transaction; the AOP annotations add cross-cutting behaviour (logging, timing, security) around methods. Both work through **proxies**.

| Annotation                     | Where It Is Used                  | Explanation                                                               |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@Transactional`               | Class / Method level              | Manages DB transactions: commit on success, rollback on **unchecked** exceptions (checked ones commit unless `rollbackFor` is set). |
| `@EnableTransactionManagement` | Class level (Configuration class) | Enables Spring’s annotation-driven transaction management.                |
| `@Aspect`                      | Class level                       | Marks a class as an Aspect (contains cross-cutting logic).                |
| `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy`      | Class level (Configuration class) | Enables AOP proxy support in Spring.                                      |
| `@Before`                      | Method level (inside Aspect)      | Runs advice before the target method executes.                            |
| `@After`                       | Method level (inside Aspect)      | Runs advice after the method finishes (success or exception).             |
| `@AfterReturning`              | Method level (inside Aspect)      | Runs after method returns successfully.                                   |
| `@AfterThrowing`               | Method level (inside Aspect)      | Runs when method throws an exception.                                     |
| `@Around`                      | Method level (inside Aspect)      | Wraps method execution (can control before & after, even skip execution). |
| `@Pointcut`                    | Method level (inside Aspect)      | Defines reusable method execution expressions.                            |
| `@Order`                       | Class level (Aspect class)        | Defines execution order when multiple aspects exist.                      |
entries.summary: @Transactional wraps a method in a database transaction; the AOP annotations add cross-cutting behaviour (logging, timing, security) around methods. Both work through proxies.

entries.question: Why doesn't `@Transactional` work when a method calls another method in the same class?
entries.answer: ↪ The call doesn't go through the Spring proxy, so no transaction (or aspect) is applied. Move the method to another bean.
entries.summary: The call doesn't go through the Spring proxy, so no transaction (or aspect) is applied. Move the method to another bean.

entries.question: What are the core Spring Boot annotations?
entries.answer:
These start the application, turn on auto-configuration, read properties, and create beans only when conditions are met.

| Annotation                       | Where It Is Used                | Explanation                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@SpringBootApplication`         | Class level                     | Main entry point. Combines `@Configuration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan`. |
| `@EnableAutoConfiguration`       | Class level                     | Automatically configures beans based on dependencies in classpath.                             |
| `@ComponentScan`                 | Class level                     | Scans packages for Spring components (beans).                                                  |
| `@Configuration`                 | Class level                     | Defines configuration class that declares beans.                                               |
| `@Bean`                          | Method level                    | Creates and registers a bean manually inside a `@Configuration` class.                         |
| `@ConfigurationProperties`       | Class level                     | Binds application properties to a POJO.                                                        |
| `@EnableConfigurationProperties` | Class level                     | Enables support for `@ConfigurationProperties` beans.                                          |
| `@Value`                         | Field / Constructor / Parameter | Injects property value from `application.properties` or `application.yml`.                     |
| `@PropertySource`                | Class level                     | Loads external `.properties` file into Spring Environment.                                     |
| `@Profile`                       | Class / Method level            | Activates beans only for specific environments (dev, prod, etc.).                              |
| `@Conditional`                   | Class / Method level            | Loads bean only if certain condition is met.                                                   |
| `@ConditionalOnProperty`         | Class / Method level            | Creates bean only if a property exists or has a specific value.                                |
| `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`      | Class / Method level            | Creates bean only if another bean is not already defined.                                      |

entries.question: What is Spring Security and why do we need it?
entries.answer:
**Spring Security** is a **framework that handles authentication, authorization, and protection against security vulnerabilities** in Spring-based applications.

Without Spring Security:

- We would manually write login logic
- We would manually protect URLs
- We might forget edge cases like CSRF, session fixation, etc.

Spring Security solves this using **filters**, **contexts**, and **standard security patterns**.

entries.question: Explain JWT authentication flow.
entries.answer:
🔐 First Understand the Big Picture

When a user logs in:

👉 Backend verifies username/password
👉 Backend generates **2 tokens**

- Access Token (short life)
- Refresh Token (long life)

Access Token and Refresh Token are two JWTs used for different purposes.

Think like this:

- 🪪 **Access token = Entry ticket**
- 🔑 **Refresh token = Ticket renewal pass**

1️⃣ When user logs in, We send both access & refresh token

```json
{
  "accessToken": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...",
  "refreshToken": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
}
```

- Purpose of Access Token is to access protected APIs.

Every API request sends:

```
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

⏳ Access Token Life: Short-lived (5–15 minutes usually)

- Purpose of Refresh Token to generate a new access token without asking user to login again.

It is like:

> “Hey server, my entry ticket expired, but I still have renewal pass.”

⏳ Refresh Token Life: Long-lived (7 days usually)

🔄 Refresh Flow:

```
Frontend → /refresh API → Send refresh token
Backend validates refresh token
Backend generates new access token
Backend sends new access token
```

```json
{
  "accessToken": "new_access_token_here"
}
```
entries.summary: First Understand the Big Picture

codeBlocks.code:
Backend validates refresh token
Backend generates new access token
Backend sends new access token

entries.question: Structure of JWT
entries.answer:
JWT = **JSON Web Token**

It has 3 parts:

```
HEADER (algorithm)
+
PAYLOAD (user data)
+
SIGNATURE (security)
```

Each part is **Base64URL-encoded** and joined with dots: `xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz`.

> ⚠️ Encoded is **not encrypted** — anyone can decode the payload (try jwt.io). Never put passwords or secrets in it. The signature only proves it **wasn't changed**.

1️⃣ Header

```json
{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}
```

2️⃣ Payload

```json
{
  "sub": "dev",
  "role": "USER",
  "iat": 1707000000,
  "exp": 1707000600
}
```

3️⃣ Signature

```
HMACSHA256(
   base64UrlEncode(header) + "." +
   base64UrlEncode(payload),
   secret_key
)
```

entries.question: Why store refresh token in HttpOnly cookie and Access Token in Memory? Why not in localstorage or sessionstorage?
entries.answer:
🔐 First Understand the Risk: XSS

XSS = Cross Site Scripting attack

If attacker injects JavaScript into your app, they can read:

```js
localStorage.getItem("token");
sessionStorage.getItem("token");
```

So anything stored there can be stolen.

⚡ Access Token in memory

- Not stored permanently
- Disappears on refresh
- Harder to steal
- Not accessible after page reload

If attacker injects script: They can only steal it while page is active.

Limited exposure.

⚡ Refresh Token in HttpOnly Cookie

- ❌ Cannot be accessed by JavaScript
- ❌ Cannot be read via localStorage
- Automatically sent by browser
- Secure + SameSite options available

entries.question: What is CSRF?
entries.answer:
**CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)** is an attack where a malicious website tricks a logged-in user’s browser into sending an unwanted request to another site.

CSRF happens when:

- User is already authenticated
- Browser automatically sends cookies
- Attacker triggers a state-changing request (POST/PUT/DELETE)

Because **cookies are automatically sent by the browser**, even if the request was triggered from another website.

**Authorization headers (Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9)** are not automatically sent, so they reduce CSRF risk.
entries.summary: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is an attack where a malicious website tricks a logged-in user’s browser into sending an unwanted request to another site.

entries.question: Why CSRF is not needed for JWT?
entries.answer:
CSRF protection is not needed for JWT because **JWT is not automatically sent by the browser**.

CSRF exploits **cookie-based authentication**:

- User logs into a site
- Browser stores session cookie
- **Browser automatically sends cookies with every request**
- Malicious site triggers a request
- Cookie is sent → request is authenticated

With JWT authentication:

- Token is stored in client-side memory (E.g `useState`, `NgRx`) or localstorage, sessionStorage
- Not stored in cookies
- Explicitly sent in headers

- Cookies are automatically sent by the browser
- That reintroduces CSRF risk
- So CSRF protection is required

Access Token - Sent via `Authorization` header, Not automatically sent by the browser, **No CSRF Protection**
Refresh Token - Automatically sent by the browser, **CSRF protection IS needed**

entries.question: Filters vs Interceptors
entries.answer:
🔹 Spring Security **Filters**

- Part of **Servlet container**
- Execute **before the request reaches the Controller**
- Used for **authentication & authorization**
- Spring Security works **mainly using filters**

📌 Examples:

- `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`
- `JwtAuthenticationFilter`

🔹 Spring MVC **Interceptors**

- Part of **Spring MVC** (`HandlerInterceptor`)
- Execute **after filters, around the controller method**: `preHandle` (before), `postHandle` (after, before the view), `afterCompletion` (at the end)
- Know **which controller method** will run, so they suit logging, auditing, locale, timing
- Not the place for security: requests that never reach a controller (static files, other servlets) skip them

🔁 Execution Flow

```
Client → Filters → Interceptors → Controller
```

✅ Simple Comparison Table

| Feature                | Filter  | Interceptor |
| ---------------------- | ------- | ----------- |
| Layer                  | Servlet | Spring MVC  |
| Runs before Controller | ✅      | ✅          |
| Can block request      | ✅ (don't call `chain.doFilter`) | ✅ (`preHandle` returns `false`) |
| Sees every request     | ✅      | ❌ only those mapped to a controller |
| Used for Security      | ✅      | ❌          |
| Spring Security uses   | Filters | ❌          |

> **Spring Security uses Filters because security must be applied before request reaches the controller.**

entries.question: What is SAML?
entries.answer:
**SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)** is an **XML-based authentication protocol** used for **Single Sign-On (SSO)**.

📌 Example:

> Login once → Access Gmail, Jira, Confluence without logging in again

🔹 How SAML Works (Simple Flow)

1. User tries to access App
2. App redirects to **Identity Provider (IdP)** (like Okta)
3. User logs in
4. IdP sends **SAML Assertion (XML)**
5. App trusts it → Login success

🔹 Why SAML?

- Used in **Enterprise applications**
- Works well with **legacy systems**
- Browser-based SSO

entries.question: Explain the OAuth2 flows — Authorization Code + PKCE and Client Credentials.
entries.answer:
OAuth2 lets an app get an **access token** without ever seeing the user's password.

**1. Authorization Code + PKCE** — for apps with a **user** (web, mobile, SPA):

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as App (client)
  participant AS as Authorization server (Keycloak, Google…)
  participant API as Resource server (your API)
  A->>A: make code_verifier, code_challenge = SHA256(verifier)
  A->>AS: redirect user to /authorize?code_challenge=…
  U->>AS: logs in, approves
  AS-->>A: redirect back with ?code=abc
  A->>AS: POST /token (code + code_verifier)
  AS-->>A: access token (+ refresh token, + ID token with OIDC)
  A->>API: GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer <token>
  API-->>A: 200 OK
```

**PKCE** ("pixie") proves the app that asks for the token is the same one that started the login, so a stolen `code` is useless.

**2. Client Credentials** — **service-to-service**, no user:

```text
Order service → POST /token (client_id + client_secret, grant_type=client_credentials)
             ← access token
Order service → Inventory API with Bearer token
```

| Flow | Use |
|---|---|
| Authorization Code + PKCE | any app with a user |
| Client Credentials | backend jobs, microservice calls |
| Device Code | TVs, CLIs |
| ~~Implicit~~, ~~Password~~ | deprecated — don't use |

**In Spring:** a login app uses `spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client` (`.oauth2Login()`); an API uses `spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server` (`.oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(...))`).

entries.question: What problems does a microservices architecture introduce, and how does Spring Cloud address those problems?
entries.answer:
**Microservices** introduce problems _because they are distributed_.
**Spring Cloud** exists to handle those distributed-system problems.

1️⃣ _PROBLEM: SERVICE LOCATION & DISCOVERY_

In microservices, **service location is dynamic**, not fixed.

- Services run on multiple machines/containers
- Containers restart → IP and port change
- Services scale up/down dynamically

**In Monolith**

```java
inventoryService.checkStock();
```

✔ Same JVM
✔ No network

**In Microservices**

```
Order Service → Network → Inventory Service
```

❌ Where is Inventory Service running?

✅ How Spring Cloud Solves It: **Service Discovery**

- Services register themselves
- Other services discover them using **logical names**

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: inventory-service
```

```java
@FeignClient(name = "inventory-service")
public interface InventoryClient {

  @GetMapping("/inventory/{id}")
  InventoryResponse check(@PathVariable Long id);
}
```

🧠 Rules to Remember

✔ Never use hardcoded URLs
✔ Service name is stable, IP is not
✔ Discovery enables load balancing

entries.question: What is @FeignClient?
entries.answer:
✖️ Problem before Feign:

1. `RestTemplate` (older, blocking)

```java
RestTemplate restTemplate = new RestTemplate();
InventoryResponse res =
  restTemplate.getForObject("http://inventory-service/inventory/1", InventoryResponse.class);
```

- Every call is hand-written: URL strings, conversions, error handling
- In **maintenance mode** (not deprecated) — for new blocking code Spring 6.1+ recommends **`RestClient`**:

```java
RestClient client = RestClient.create("http://inventory-service");
InventoryResponse res = client.get().uri("/inventory/{id}", 1).retrieve().body(InventoryResponse.class);
```

2. WebClient (reactive, non-blocking)

```java
WebClient webClient = WebClient.create();

InventoryResponse res =
  webClient.get()
           .uri("http://inventory-service/inventory/1")
           .retrieve()
           .bodyToMono(InventoryResponse.class)
           .block();
```

✔ Non-blocking
✔ High performance
✖️ More code
✖️ Overkill for simple sync calls

✔️ `@FeignClient` is a Spring Cloud annotation used to declare a **type-safe HTTP client** for calling another microservice **by service name**, not by URL.

- It lets you call a remote REST API as if it were a local Java method.

`@EnableFeignClients` - Enables Feign in the application.

```java
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableFeignClients
public class OrderServiceApplication { }

@FeignClient(
  name = "inventory-service",        // ALWAYS - Without this, Feign is useless in microservices.
  path = "/inventory",               // SOMETIMES - Avoid repeating /inventory in every method
  configuration = InventoryFeignConfig.class, // SOMETIMES - Don’t overuse — keep configs minimal.
  fallback = InventoryFallback.class,          // RARE - Never use fallback and fallbackFactory together.
  fallbackFactory = InventoryFallbackFactory.class // PREFERRED - Always prefer this for production
)
public interface InventoryClient {}
```

> **`Feign`** is blocking. For high-throughput or streaming use cases, **`WebClient`** is more suitable.
>
> 💡 Spring Cloud OpenFeign is now feature-complete (maintenance mode). Spring's own alternative is the **HTTP interface client**: an interface with `@GetExchange("/inventory/{id}")` methods, backed by `RestClient` or `WebClient`.

2️⃣ _PROBLEM: CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT_

In microservices, **configuration grows faster than code**.

❌ Without central config:

- Rebuild required
- Inconsistent configs
- Manual errors

✅ How Spring Cloud Solves It: **Config Server**

- Centralized configuration
- Environment-based configs
- Same binary everywhere

```yaml
spring:
  cloud:
    config:
      uri: http://config-server:8888
```

Config stored in Git:

```
order-service-dev.yml
order-service-prod.yml
```

3️⃣ _PROBLEM: NETWORK FAILURES & CASCADING FAILURES_

❌ In microservices, **network calls are unreliable by default**.

- Network latency
- Service downtime
- Slow responses block threads

Without protection:

```java
inventoryClient.checkStock(id); // blocks indefinitely
```

✖️ Thread pool exhaustion
✖️ System-wide slowdown

✅ How Spring Cloud Solves It: **Resilience**

- Detect failures
- Stop repeated calls
- Degrade gracefully

```java
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "fallback")
public InventoryResponse checkStock(Long productId) {
    return inventoryClient.checkStock(productId);
}

public InventoryResponse fallback(Long productId, Throwable ex) {
    return new InventoryResponse(productId, false);
}
```

entries.question: What do you mean by resilience in a microservices system?
entries.answer:
> Resilience is the ability of a system to continue functioning gracefully in the presence of partial failures, slow dependencies, or transient network issues.

- Failures are **expected**, not exceptional
- Resilience is about **containing failures**
- Goal is **system stability**, not perfect success

entries.question: Why do we need resilience patterns in microservices but not in monoliths?
entries.answer:
In a **monolith**:

- Method calls are in-process
- No network latency
- Failures are centralized

In **microservices**:

- Remote calls over network
- Independent scaling
- Partial failures are common

> Microservices fail independently, monoliths fail together.

entries.question: Which resilience patterns do you commonly use?
entries.answer:

- **Retry** – transient failures
- **Circuit Breaker** – persistent failures
- **Bulkhead** – isolate resources
- **Fallback** – graceful degradation

✔ Timeout is non-negotiable
✔ Retry without breaker is dangerous
✔ Fallback must be meaningful

entries.question: Explain Circuit Breaker using a real scenario.
entries.answer:

- Prevents repeated calls to failing service

entries.question: How do you enable distributed tracing in Spring Boot?
entries.answer:
In Spring Boot 3, **Micrometer Tracing** replaced Spring Cloud Sleuth. Add Actuator, a tracer bridge and an exporter:

```xml
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>io.micrometer</groupId><artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave</artifactId></dependency>   <!-- or -bridge-otel -->
<dependency><groupId>io.zipkin.reporter2</groupId><artifactId>zipkin-reporter-brave</artifactId></dependency>
```

Then set the sampling rate:

```yaml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0
```

- Sampling controls overhead
- `1.0` → trace everything (dev/test)
- Lower in production

🧠 RULES

✔ Full sampling in non-prod
✔ Reduced sampling in prod
✔ Tracing has overhead

entries.question: How Load Balancing Works in Spring Boot?
entries.answer:
> **Spring Boot = Business Logic** > **Spring Cloud / Platform = Load Balancing** 🧠 Case 1: Using Spring Cloud Spring Boot uses **Spring Cloud LoadBalancer** when: - You call another service using **service name** instead of IP - A **Service Registry** is present Example registries: - **Eureka** - **Consul** - **Kubernetes Service Discovery** ✅ Flow 1. Service instances register themselves 2. Client asks for `USER-SERVICE` 3. LoadBalancer picks **one healthy instance** 4. Request is forwarded ```mermaid flowchart LR U1[user-service #1] -. registers .-> REG[(Service registry
Eureka / Consul)] U2[user-service #2] -. registers .-> REG C[Caller service] -- "http://USER-SERVICE" --> LB[Spring Cloud LoadBalancer] LB -- asks for instances --> REG LB -- round robin --> U1 LB -- round robin --> U2 ``` 🔹 **Simple Code Example (Client-Side Load Balancing)** ✅ Dependency ```xml org.springframework.cloud spring-cloud-starter-loadbalancer ``` ✅ RestTemplate with Load Balancer ```java @Bean @LoadBalanced public RestTemplate restTemplate() { return new RestTemplate(); } ``` ✅ Calling Another Service ```java String response = restTemplate.getForObject( "http://ORDER-SERVICE/orders", String.class); ``` 👉 **ORDER-SERVICE** is resolved dynamically to: ``` 10.0.1.2 10.0.1.3 10.0.1.4 ``` 🔹 **Load Balancing Strategy** Default strategy: ``` Round Robin ``` Other strategies: - Random - Weighted - Custom

entries.question: When would you avoid synchronous REST calls between services?
entries.answer:
Avoid a synchronous call when the caller **doesn't need the answer right now**, or when waiting would make one slow service slow everyone:

| Situation | Why REST hurts |
|---|---|
| Long chains (A → B → C → D) | Latencies add up; any failure breaks the whole request |
| Fan-out to many services | One slow service delays the response |
| Work that can happen later (emails, reports, analytics) | The user waits for something they don't need yet |
| Spiky traffic | A sudden burst overloads the downstream service |

Use **events or a queue** instead (Kafka / RabbitMQ):

**Sync (slow, fragile):**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[Order] -- wait --> P[Payment] -- wait --> E[Email] --> R[Reply to user]
```

**Async (fast, independent):**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[Order] -- "publish OrderPlaced" --> K[(Kafka / RabbitMQ)]
  O --> R[Reply to user immediately]
  K --> P[Payment service]
  K --> E[Email service]
```

Keep REST for **queries that need an immediate answer** ("is this item in stock?"), with timeouts and a circuit breaker.

**Rule of thumb:** sync is simple but risky; async is scalable and resilient; critical multi-step workflows → events.
entries.summary: Avoid a synchronous call when the caller doesn't need the answer right now, or when waiting would make one slow service slow everyone:

flowchart LR
  O[Order] -- "publish OrderPlaced" --> K[(Kafka / RabbitMQ)]
  O --> R[Reply to user immediately]
  K --> P[Payment service]
  K --> E[Email service]
