entries.question: What is SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle)?
entries.answer: **SDLC** (Software Development Life Cycle) — A structured process for building and maintaining software, in stages: requirements → design → development → testing → deployment → maintenance. It helps teams plan work, keep quality high and deliver predictably. Example: a banking app goes through all six stages before and after each release.
entries.summary: SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) — A structured process for building and maintaining software, in stages: requirements → design → development → testing → deployment → maintenance. It helps teams plan work, keep quality high and deliver predictably. Example: a banking app goes through all six stages before and…

entries.question: What is STLC (Software Testing Life Cycle)?
entries.answer: **STLC** (Software Testing Life Cycle) — The testing side of the SDLC: requirement analysis → test planning → test case design → environment setup → execution → closure. It makes testing planned and measurable instead of ad hoc. Example: QA writes test cases from the login story before developers finish coding it.
entries.summary: STLC (Software Testing Life Cycle) — The testing side of the SDLC: requirement analysis → test planning → test case design → environment setup → execution → closure. It makes testing planned and measurable instead of ad hoc. Example: QA writes test cases from the login story before developers finish coding it.

entries.question: What is Environment?
entries.answer: **Environment** — A separate copy of the system used for one purpose, so work in progress never breaks what real users see. Code moves step by step: DEV (developers) → QA/TEST (testers) → UAT (business users) → STAGING (production-like rehearsal) → PROD (live). Each has its own database and settings.
entries.summary: Environment — A separate copy of the system used for one purpose, so work in progress never breaks what real users see. Code moves step by step: DEV (developers) → QA/TEST (testers) → UAT (business users) → STAGING (production-like rehearsal) → PROD (live). Each has its own database and settings.

entries.question: What is Production (Prod)?
entries.answer: **Production (Prod)** — The live system that real customers use, with real data and money. Changes reach it only after testing in lower environments, usually through an approved release. Example: a bug in PROD affects every user, so teams fix it with a hotfix and a postmortem.
entries.summary: Production (Prod) — The live system that real customers use, with real data and money. Changes reach it only after testing in lower environments, usually through an approved release. Example: a bug in PROD affects every user, so teams fix it with a hotfix and a postmortem.

entries.question: What is UAT (User Acceptance Testing)?
entries.answer: **UAT** (User Acceptance Testing) — The final testing stage, where business users check that the software solves their real problem before release. Developers and QA confirm it works; UAT confirms it is what the business wanted. Example: the finance team runs month-end reports in UAT and signs off before go-live.
entries.summary: UAT (User Acceptance Testing) — The final testing stage, where business users check that the software solves their real problem before release. Developers and QA confirm it works; UAT confirms it is what the business wanted. Example: the finance team runs month-end reports in UAT and signs off before go-live.

entries.question: What is POC (Proof of Concept)?
entries.answer: **POC** (Proof of Concept) — A small, quick experiment to prove an idea or technology works before investing in it. It is thrown away or rebuilt properly afterwards; it is not meant for users. Example: a 2-week POC checks whether an LLM can read invoices accurately before the full project is approved.
entries.summary: POC (Proof of Concept) — A small, quick experiment to prove an idea or technology works before investing in it. It is thrown away or rebuilt properly afterwards; it is not meant for users. Example: a 2-week POC checks whether an LLM can read invoices accurately before the full project is approved.

entries.question: What is MVP (Minimum Viable Product)?
entries.answer: **MVP** (Minimum Viable Product) — The smallest version of a product with just enough features for real users to use and give feedback. It lets a team learn what customers want before building everything. Example: a food-delivery MVP has ordering and payment only — no ratings, offers or tracking yet.
entries.summary: MVP (Minimum Viable Product) — The smallest version of a product with just enough features for real users to use and give feedback. It lets a team learn what customers want before building everything. Example: a food-delivery MVP has ordering and payment only — no ratings, offers or tracking yet.

entries.question: What is Hotfix / Patch?
entries.answer: **Hotfix / Patch** — An urgent fix released straight to production, outside the normal release schedule, for a serious bug or security issue. It is kept small to reduce risk and then merged back into the main branch. Example: a payment failure on sale day gets a same-day hotfix.
entries.summary: Hotfix / Patch — An urgent fix released straight to production, outside the normal release schedule, for a serious bug or security issue. It is kept small to reduce risk and then merged back into the main branch. Example: a payment failure on sale day gets a same-day hotfix.

entries.question: What is Semantic Versioning (SemVer)?
entries.answer: **Semantic Versioning** (SemVer) — A version number format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH that tells users how risky an upgrade is. MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = new feature that is backward compatible, PATCH = bug fix. Example: 2.4.1 → 2.5.0 is safe to upgrade; 2.x → 3.0.0 may need code changes.
entries.summary: Semantic Versioning (SemVer) — A version number format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH that tells users how risky an upgrade is. MAJOR = breaking change, MINOR = new feature that is backward compatible, PATCH = bug fix. Example: 2.4.1 → 2.5.0 is safe to upgrade; 2.x → 3.0.0 may need code changes.

entries.question: What is Version Control / Git?
entries.answer: **Version Control / Git** — A system that records every change to code over time, so a team can work together, see history and undo mistakes. Git is the standard tool, and GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket host Git repositories online. Example: git log shows who changed a file, when and why.
entries.summary: Version Control / Git — A system that records every change to code over time, so a team can work together, see history and undo mistakes. Git is the standard tool, and GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket host Git repositories online. Example: git log shows who changed a file, when and why.

entries.question: What is Branch / Merge / PR?
entries.answer: **Branch / Merge / PR** — A branch is a separate line of work so you can change code without disturbing others; a merge combines it back. A PR (Pull Request) asks teammates to review the branch before merging. Example: feature/login branch → PR → review and tests pass → merge into main.
entries.summary: Branch / Merge / PR — A branch is a separate line of work so you can change code without disturbing others; a merge combines it back. A PR (Pull Request) asks teammates to review the branch before merging. Example: feature/login branch → PR → review and tests pass → merge into main.

entries.question: What is Commit?
entries.answer: **Commit** — A saved snapshot of your changes in Git, with a message, author, time and a unique ID (hash). Small commits with clear messages make history easy to read and changes easy to undo. Example: git commit -m "Fix tax rounding on payslip".
entries.summary: Commit — A saved snapshot of your changes in Git, with a message, author, time and a unique ID (hash). Small commits with clear messages make history easy to read and changes easy to undo. Example: git commit -m "Fix tax rounding on payslip".

entries.question: What is Clone / Fork?
entries.answer: **Clone / Fork** — Clone makes a full local copy of a repository on your machine. Fork makes your own copy of someone else's repository on the server, so you can change it and send back a pull request. Example: fork an open-source library on GitHub, clone your fork, fix a bug, open a PR.
entries.summary: Clone / Fork — Clone makes a full local copy of a repository on your machine. Fork makes your own copy of someone else's repository on the server, so you can change it and send back a pull request. Example: fork an open-source library on GitHub, clone your fork, fix a bug, open a PR.

entries.question: What is Rebase?
entries.answer: **Rebase** — Moves your commits so they sit on top of the latest version of another branch, giving a straight, linear history. It rewrites commit IDs, so never rebase commits others are already using. Example: git rebase main updates your feature branch with the newest main before a PR.
entries.summary: Rebase — Moves your commits so they sit on top of the latest version of another branch, giving a straight, linear history. It rewrites commit IDs, so never rebase commits others are already using. Example: git rebase main updates your feature branch with the newest main before a PR.

entries.question: What is Merge Conflict?
entries.answer: **Merge Conflict** — Happens when two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot decide which version to keep. You open the file, pick or combine the changes, then commit. Example: two developers both edit the same price formula — Git marks both versions for you to resolve.
entries.summary: Merge Conflict — Happens when two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot decide which version to keep. You open the file, pick or combine the changes, then commit. Example: two developers both edit the same price formula — Git marks both versions for you to resolve.

entries.question: What is Tag?
entries.answer: **Tag** — A permanent name attached to one commit, usually to mark a release. Unlike a branch it doesn't move, so you can always rebuild exactly what shipped. Example: tag v1.4.0 marks the commit deployed to production on release day.
entries.summary: Tag — A permanent name attached to one commit, usually to mark a release. Unlike a branch it doesn't move, so you can always rebuild exactly what shipped. Example: tag v1.4.0 marks the commit deployed to production on release day.

entries.question: What is Legacy System?
entries.answer: **Legacy System** — An old system still running important business work, often built with outdated technology and few people who understand it. It is risky to change but too critical to switch off. Example: a 25-year-old COBOL mainframe that still processes a bank's daily transactions.
entries.summary: Legacy System — An old system still running important business work, often built with outdated technology and few people who understand it. It is risky to change but too critical to switch off. Example: a 25-year-old COBOL mainframe that still processes a bank's daily transactions.

entries.question: What is Technical Debt?
entries.answer: **Technical Debt** — The future cost of taking shortcuts today — quick fixes, missing tests or messy design that slow every later change. Like financial debt, it grows 'interest' until you pay it back by refactoring. Example: copying the same validation into 10 places means a rule change now needs 10 edits.
entries.summary: Technical Debt — The future cost of taking shortcuts today — quick fixes, missing tests or messy design that slow every later change. Like financial debt, it grows 'interest' until you pay it back by refactoring. Example: copying the same validation into 10 places means a rule change now needs 10 edits.

entries.question: What is Refactoring?
entries.answer: **Refactoring** — Improving the internal structure of code without changing what it does for users. It makes code easier to read, test and change, and is safest with good tests in place. Example: splitting a 500-line method into small named methods with the same output.
entries.summary: Refactoring — Improving the internal structure of code without changing what it does for users. It makes code easier to read, test and change, and is safest with good tests in place. Example: splitting a 500-line method into small named methods with the same output.

entries.question: What is IDE (Integrated Development Environment)?
entries.answer: **IDE** (Integrated Development Environment) — A code editor with built-in tools to write, run, debug and refactor code in one place. It adds autocomplete, error highlighting and Git integration to save time. Examples: IntelliJ IDEA for Java, VS Code for web, Eclipse, Android Studio.
entries.summary: IDE (Integrated Development Environment) — A code editor with built-in tools to write, run, debug and refactor code in one place. It adds autocomplete, error highlighting and Git integration to save time. Examples: IntelliJ IDEA for Java, VS Code for web, Eclipse, Android Studio.

entries.question: What is SDK (Software Development Kit)?
entries.answer: **SDK** (Software Development Kit) — A ready-made kit of libraries, tools and docs for building software on a particular platform or service. It saves you from writing low-level code yourself. Example: the AWS SDK for Java lets you upload a file to S3 with one method call.
entries.summary: SDK (Software Development Kit) — A ready-made kit of libraries, tools and docs for building software on a particular platform or service. It saves you from writing low-level code yourself. Example: the AWS SDK for Java lets you upload a file to S3 with one method call.

entries.question: What is Library vs Framework?
entries.answer: **Library vs Framework** — With a library, your code is in charge and calls it when needed. With a framework, the framework is in charge and calls your code at the right time (inversion of control). Example: you call Lodash functions yourself; Spring Boot calls your @RestController methods when requests arrive.
entries.summary: Library vs Framework — With a library, your code is in charge and calls it when needed. With a framework, the framework is in charge and calls your code at the right time (inversion of control). Example: you call Lodash functions yourself; Spring Boot calls your @RestController methods when requests arrive.

entries.question: What is Open Source?
entries.answer: **Open Source** — Software whose source code is public, so anyone can use, study and improve it under its licence. Licences differ — MIT/Apache allow almost anything, GPL requires sharing your changes. Examples: Linux, Kubernetes, React, PostgreSQL.
entries.summary: Open Source — Software whose source code is public, so anyone can use, study and improve it under its licence. Licences differ — MIT/Apache allow almost anything, GPL requires sharing your changes. Examples: Linux, Kubernetes, React, PostgreSQL.

entries.question: What is Compiled vs Interpreted?
entries.answer: **Compiled vs Interpreted** — Compiled languages are turned into machine code before running, so they start and run fast (C, Go, Rust). Interpreted languages are run by another program as they go (Python, classic JavaScript). Java and C# are in between: compiled to bytecode, then run and optimised by a virtual machine (JIT).
entries.summary: Compiled vs Interpreted — Compiled languages are turned into machine code before running, so they start and run fast (C, Go, Rust). Interpreted languages are run by another program as they go (Python, classic JavaScript). Java and C# are in between: compiled to bytecode, then run and optimised by a virtual machine…

entries.question: What is Runtime?
entries.answer: **Runtime** — The environment that actually runs your program and provides memory management, threads and standard libraries. Your code needs the right runtime installed to run. Examples: JVM for Java, Node.js for server JavaScript, .NET CLR for C#, the browser for front-end JavaScript.
entries.summary: Runtime — The environment that actually runs your program and provides memory management, threads and standard libraries. Your code needs the right runtime installed to run. Examples: JVM for Java, Node.js for server JavaScript, .NET CLR for C#, the browser for front-end JavaScript.

entries.question: What is DOM (Document Object Model)?
entries.answer: **DOM** (Document Object Model) — The browser's tree of objects built from a page's HTML; each tag becomes a node JavaScript can read and change. Changing the DOM updates what the user sees without reloading. Example: document.getElementById('total').textContent = '₹500' updates the price on screen.
entries.summary: DOM (Document Object Model) — The browser's tree of objects built from a page's HTML; each tag becomes a node JavaScript can read and change. Changing the DOM updates what the user sees without reloading. Example: document.getElementById('total').textContent = '₹500' updates the price on screen.

entries.question: What is SPA (Single Page Application)?
entries.answer: **SPA** (Single Page Application) — A web app that loads one HTML page once and then swaps content with JavaScript instead of reloading pages. It feels fast like a desktop app, but needs extra work for SEO and first load. Examples: Gmail, and most Angular or React apps.
entries.summary: SPA (Single Page Application) — A web app that loads one HTML page once and then swaps content with JavaScript instead of reloading pages. It feels fast like a desktop app, but needs extra work for SEO and first load. Examples: Gmail, and most Angular or React apps.

entries.question: What is SSR / CSR / SSG?
entries.answer: **SSR / CSR / SSG** — Three ways to build a page's HTML. CSR: the browser builds it with JavaScript; SSR: the server builds it per request (faster first view, better SEO); SSG: HTML is built once at deploy time (fastest, for content that rarely changes). Example: blog → SSG, dashboard → CSR, e-commerce product page → SSR.
entries.summary: SSR / CSR / SSG — Three ways to build a page's HTML. CSR: the browser builds it with JavaScript; SSR: the server builds it per request (faster first view, better SEO); SSG: HTML is built once at deploy time (fastest, for content that rarely changes). Example: blog → SSG, dashboard → CSR, e-commerce product page → SSR.

entries.question: What is Responsive Design?
entries.answer: **Responsive Design** — Designing one website that adjusts its layout to any screen size — phone, tablet or desktop. It uses flexible grids, relative units and CSS media queries. Example: a three-column desktop layout becomes a single column on a phone.
entries.summary: Responsive Design — Designing one website that adjusts its layout to any screen size — phone, tablet or desktop. It uses flexible grids, relative units and CSS media queries. Example: a three-column desktop layout becomes a single column on a phone.

entries.question: What is Component?
entries.answer: **Component** — A reusable, self-contained piece of UI with its own template, styles and logic. Pages are built by combining components, so a fix in one place applies everywhere it is used. Example: one <product-card> component used on the home, search and wishlist pages.
entries.summary: Component — A reusable, self-contained piece of UI with its own template, styles and logic. Pages are built by combining components, so a fix in one place applies everywhere it is used. Example: one component used on the home, search and wishlist pages.

entries.question: What is State Management?
entries.answer: **State Management** — Keeping data shared by many parts of the UI (logged-in user, cart, filters) in one predictable place. It prevents screens showing different values for the same data. Tools: NgRx or Signals (Angular), Redux or Zustand (React). Example: adding an item updates the cart badge and the cart page together.
entries.summary: State Management — Keeping data shared by many parts of the UI (logged-in user, cart, filters) in one predictable place. It prevents screens showing different values for the same data. Tools: NgRx or Signals (Angular), Redux or Zustand (React). Example: adding an item updates the cart badge and the cart page together.

entries.question: What is Accessibility (a11y)?
entries.answer: **Accessibility (a11y)** — Making apps usable by everyone, including people using screen readers, keyboards only or with low vision. It follows the WCAG standard and is a legal requirement in many countries. Example: alt text on images, visible focus outlines and enough colour contrast.
entries.summary: Accessibility (a11y) — Making apps usable by everyone, including people using screen readers, keyboards only or with low vision. It follows the WCAG standard and is a legal requirement in many countries. Example: alt text on images, visible focus outlines and enough colour contrast.

entries.question: What is Core Web Vitals?
entries.answer: **Core Web Vitals** — Google's three metrics for real user experience: LCP (main content loads in under 2.5 s), INP (page responds to clicks in under 200 ms) and CLS (layout doesn't jump, under 0.1). They affect search ranking. Example: reserving space for images stops content jumping and improves CLS.
entries.summary: Core Web Vitals — Google's three metrics for real user experience: LCP (main content loads in under 2.5 s), INP (page responds to clicks in under 200 ms) and CLS (layout doesn't jump, under 0.1). They affect search ranking. Example: reserving space for images stops content jumping and improves CLS.

entries.question: What is Bundler?
entries.answer: **Bundler** — A build tool that combines many JavaScript/CSS files and packages into a few optimised files for the browser. It also minifies code, removes unused code and splits bundles for faster loading. Examples: Vite, Webpack, esbuild (Angular's build uses esbuild).
entries.summary: Bundler — A build tool that combines many JavaScript/CSS files and packages into a few optimised files for the browser. It also minifies code, removes unused code and splits bundles for faster loading. Examples: Vite, Webpack, esbuild (Angular's build uses esbuild).

entries.question: What is PWA (Progressive Web App)?
entries.answer: **PWA** (Progressive Web App) — A website that behaves like an installed app — it can work offline, be added to the home screen and send notifications. It uses a service worker and a web manifest. Example: Starbucks and Twitter/X offer PWAs that work on slow or no network.
entries.summary: PWA (Progressive Web App) — A website that behaves like an installed app — it can work offline, be added to the home screen and send notifications. It uses a service worker and a web manifest. Example: Starbucks and Twitter/X offer PWAs that work on slow or no network.

entries.question: What is Design System?
entries.answer: **Design System** — A shared library of UI components, colours, fonts and usage rules that keeps every screen consistent. Designers and developers build from the same parts, so work is faster and the product looks unified. Examples: Google's Material Design, IBM Carbon.
entries.summary: Design System — A shared library of UI components, colours, fonts and usage rules that keeps every screen consistent. Designers and developers build from the same parts, so work is faster and the product looks unified. Examples: Google's Material Design, IBM Carbon.

entries.question: What is Lazy Loading?
entries.answer: **Lazy Loading** — Loading code, images or data only when they are actually needed, instead of everything at startup. It makes the first page load faster and saves data. Example: an Angular admin module or below-the-fold images load only when the user navigates or scrolls to them.
entries.summary: Lazy Loading — Loading code, images or data only when they are actually needed, instead of everything at startup. It makes the first page load faster and saves data. Example: an Angular admin module or below-the-fold images load only when the user navigates or scrolls to them.

entries.question: What is API (Application Programming Interface)?
entries.answer: **API** (Application Programming Interface) — A defined contract that lets one program request data or actions from another without knowing how it works inside. It specifies the requests you can make and the responses you get. Example: a weather app calls GET /weather?city=Chennai and receives JSON with the temperature.
entries.summary: API (Application Programming Interface) — A defined contract that lets one program request data or actions from another without knowing how it works inside. It specifies the requests you can make and the responses you get. Example: a weather app calls GET /weather?city=Chennai and receives JSON with the temperature.

entries.question: What is REST (Representational State Transfer)?
entries.answer: **REST** (Representational State Transfer) — A popular style for web APIs where everything is a resource with a URL, and HTTP methods say what to do: GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove. It is simple, stateless and works over plain HTTP with JSON. Example: GET /api/orders/42 returns order 42.
entries.summary: REST (Representational State Transfer) — A popular style for web APIs where everything is a resource with a URL, and HTTP methods say what to do: GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove. It is simple, stateless and works over plain HTTP with JSON. Example: GET /api/orders/42 returns order 42.

entries.question: What is GraphQL?
entries.answer: **GraphQL** — An API query language where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request, through a single endpoint. It avoids over-fetching and multiple round trips, but caching and security need more care. Example: a mobile app requests just a user's name and last 3 orders in one query.
entries.summary: GraphQL — An API query language where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request, through a single endpoint. It avoids over-fetching and multiple round trips, but caching and security need more care. Example: a mobile app requests just a user's name and last 3 orders in one query.

entries.question: What is gRPC?
entries.answer: **gRPC** — A fast API framework from Google that sends compact binary messages (Protocol Buffers) over HTTP/2. It generates client and server code from a .proto contract and supports streaming. Common for service-to-service calls where speed matters; browsers need a proxy to use it.
entries.summary: gRPC — A fast API framework from Google that sends compact binary messages (Protocol Buffers) over HTTP/2. It generates client and server code from a .proto contract and supports streaming. Common for service-to-service calls where speed matters; browsers need a proxy to use it.

entries.question: What is Webhook?
entries.answer: **Webhook** — A callback where a service sends an HTTP request to your URL as soon as an event happens, instead of you checking repeatedly (polling). You register the URL once and verify each call's signature. Example: Razorpay calls your /payment-webhook when a payment succeeds.
entries.summary: Webhook — A callback where a service sends an HTTP request to your URL as soon as an event happens, instead of you checking repeatedly (polling). You register the URL once and verify each call's signature. Example: Razorpay calls your /payment-webhook when a payment succeeds.

entries.question: What is WebSocket?
entries.answer: **WebSocket** — A connection that stays open so the server and browser can send messages to each other at any time. Unlike normal HTTP, the server can push updates without being asked. Used for chat, live scores, trading prices and multiplayer games.
entries.summary: WebSocket — A connection that stays open so the server and browser can send messages to each other at any time. Unlike normal HTTP, the server can push updates without being asked. Used for chat, live scores, trading prices and multiplayer games.

entries.question: What is JSON / XML / YAML?
entries.answer: **JSON / XML / YAML** — Text formats for structured data. JSON is light and the default for APIs; XML is verbose with tags, still used in banking, SOAP and older systems; YAML is indentation-based and used for config files. Example: {"id": 1} in JSON; a Kubernetes deployment written in YAML.
entries.summary: JSON / XML / YAML — Text formats for structured data. JSON is light and the default for APIs; XML is verbose with tags, still used in banking, SOAP and older systems; YAML is indentation-based and used for config files. Example: {"id": 1} in JSON; a Kubernetes deployment written in YAML.

entries.question: What is HTTP Status Codes?
entries.answer: **HTTP Status Codes** — Three-digit codes in every HTTP response that say what happened. 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 forbidden, 404 not found), 5xx server error (500, 503). Correct codes help clients and monitoring react properly.
entries.summary: HTTP Status Codes — Three-digit codes in every HTTP response that say what happened. 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 forbidden, 404 not found), 5xx server error (500, 503). Correct codes help clients and monitoring react properly.

entries.question: What is Endpoint?
entries.answer: **Endpoint** — One specific URL plus HTTP method that an API exposes for one operation. An API is a collection of endpoints. Example: GET /api/orders lists orders, POST /api/orders creates one, GET /api/orders/42 fetches order 42.
entries.summary: Endpoint — One specific URL plus HTTP method that an API exposes for one operation. An API is a collection of endpoints. Example: GET /api/orders lists orders, POST /api/orders creates one, GET /api/orders/42 fetches order 42.

entries.question: What is Middleware?
entries.answer: **Middleware** — Code that runs between receiving a request and sending the response, to handle common work like logging, authentication or compression. The term also means software that connects separate systems (message brokers, integration tools). Example: an Express middleware that checks the JWT before every route.
entries.summary: Middleware — Code that runs between receiving a request and sending the response, to handle common work like logging, authentication or compression. The term also means software that connects separate systems (message brokers, integration tools). Example: an Express middleware that checks the JWT before every route.

entries.question: What is ORM (Object-Relational Mapping)?
entries.answer: **ORM** (Object-Relational Mapping) — A library that maps database tables to classes and rows to objects, so you work with objects instead of writing most SQL by hand. It saves code but can hide slow queries (like the N+1 problem). Examples: Hibernate/JPA (Java), Entity Framework (.NET), Prisma (Node.js).
entries.summary: ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) — A library that maps database tables to classes and rows to objects, so you work with objects instead of writing most SQL by hand. It saves code but can hide slow queries (like the N+1 problem). Examples: Hibernate/JPA (Java), Entity Framework (.NET), Prisma (Node.js).

entries.question: What is Dependency Injection (DI)?
entries.answer: **Dependency Injection (DI)** — A design where an object receives the things it needs (its dependencies) from outside instead of creating them itself. This makes code loosely coupled and easy to test with mocks. Example: Spring passes a PaymentService into OrderService's constructor; in tests you pass a fake one.
entries.summary: Dependency Injection (DI) — A design where an object receives the things it needs (its dependencies) from outside instead of creating them itself. This makes code loosely coupled and easy to test with mocks. Example: Spring passes a PaymentService into OrderService's constructor; in tests you pass a fake one.

entries.question: What is OOP (Object-Oriented Programming)?
entries.answer: **OOP** (Object-Oriented Programming) — A way of organising code as objects that bundle data with the methods that work on it. Its four pillars are encapsulation (protect data), abstraction (hide details), inheritance (reuse) and polymorphism (one interface, many forms). Example: a BankAccount class keeps balance private and changes it only through deposit() and withdraw().

Its four pillars are encapsulation (protect data), abstraction (hide details), inheritance (reuse) and polymorphism (one interface, many forms). Example: a BankAccount class keeps balance private…

entries.question: What is SOLID?
entries.answer: **SOLID** — Five principles for code that is easy to change: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion. Following them keeps classes small, focused and loosely coupled. Example: adding a new payment type by adding a class, without editing existing ones (open/closed).

Following them keeps classes small, focused and loosely coupled. Example: adding a new payment type by adding a class, without editing existing ones…

entries.question: What is Design Patterns?
entries.answer: **Design Patterns** — Proven, named solutions to common design problems, so teams don't reinvent them and can talk in shared terms. Examples: Singleton (one instance), Factory (create objects), Builder (step-by-step construction), Strategy (swap algorithms), Observer (notify listeners), Adapter (make interfaces fit).
entries.summary: Design Patterns — Proven, named solutions to common design problems, so teams don't reinvent them and can talk in shared terms. Examples: Singleton (one instance), Factory (create objects), Builder (step-by-step construction), Strategy (swap algorithms), Observer (notify listeners), Adapter (make interfaces fit).

entries.question: What is Concurrency / Multithreading?
entries.answer: **Concurrency / Multithreading** — Running several tasks at overlapping times, often on multiple threads, to use CPUs fully and keep apps responsive. The hard part is shared data — without locks or thread-safe structures you get race conditions. Example: a server handles 200 requests at once, each on its own thread.
entries.summary: Concurrency / Multithreading — Running several tasks at overlapping times, often on multiple threads, to use CPUs fully and keep apps responsive. The hard part is shared data — without locks or thread-safe structures you get race conditions. Example: a server handles 200 requests at once, each on its own thread.

entries.question: What is Idempotency?
entries.answer: **Idempotency** — An operation is idempotent if doing it once or many times has the same effect. It makes retries safe after timeouts and network errors. Example: a payment API takes an idempotency key, so a retried 'pay ₹500' request charges the customer only once.
entries.summary: Idempotency — An operation is idempotent if doing it once or many times has the same effect. It makes retries safe after timeouts and network errors. Example: a payment API takes an idempotency key, so a retried 'pay ₹500' request charges the customer only once.

entries.question: What is Rate Limiting?
entries.answer: **Rate Limiting** — Limiting how many requests a client can make in a time window, to protect a service from overload and abuse. Extra requests get HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Example: a public API allows 100 requests per minute per API key.
entries.summary: Rate Limiting — Limiting how many requests a client can make in a time window, to protect a service from overload and abuse. Extra requests get HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Example: a public API allows 100 requests per minute per API key.

entries.question: What is Swagger / OpenAPI?
entries.answer: **Swagger / OpenAPI** — OpenAPI is a standard format (YAML/JSON) for describing a REST API's endpoints, inputs and outputs; Swagger is the popular toolset around it. From one spec you get interactive docs, client code and contract tests. Example: Spring Boot with springdoc shows a Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html.
entries.summary: Swagger / OpenAPI — OpenAPI is a standard format (YAML/JSON) for describing a REST API's endpoints, inputs and outputs; Swagger is the popular toolset around it. From one spec you get interactive docs, client code and contract tests. Example: Spring Boot with springdoc shows a Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html.

entries.question: What is Big-O Notation?
entries.answer: **Big-O Notation** — Describes how an algorithm's time or memory grows as the input grows, ignoring constants. Common classes, fastest to slowest: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²). Example: finding an item in a HashMap is O(1); searching an unsorted list is O(n).

entries.question: What is DSA (Data Structures & Algorithms)?
entries.answer: **DSA** (Data Structures & Algorithms) — Data structures (arrays, lists, stacks, queues, hash maps, trees, graphs) are ways to store data; algorithms (sorting, searching, traversal, dynamic programming) are ways to process it. Choosing the right pair makes programs fast, and DSA is the core of coding interviews. Example: use a HashSet to find duplicates in O(n).

entries.question: What is Monolith?
entries.answer: **Monolith** — An application built, tested and deployed as one single unit, with all features in one codebase. It is simple to start and debug, but becomes slow to change and scale as teams and code grow. Example: one Spring Boot app containing users, orders, payments and reports.
entries.summary: Monolith — An application built, tested and deployed as one single unit, with all features in one codebase. It is simple to start and debug, but becomes slow to change and scale as teams and code grow. Example: one Spring Boot app containing users, orders, payments and reports.

entries.question: What is Microservices?
entries.answer: **Microservices** — An architecture where a system is split into small services, each owning one business area and its own data, deployed independently. Teams can release and scale services separately, at the cost of network calls, distributed data and more operations work. Example: separate order, payment and inventory services.
entries.summary: Microservices — An architecture where a system is split into small services, each owning one business area and its own data, deployed independently. Teams can release and scale services separately, at the cost of network calls, distributed data and more operations work. Example: separate order, payment and inventory…

entries.question: What is Modular Monolith?
entries.answer: **Modular Monolith** — A single deployable application divided into strict modules that communicate only through clear interfaces. You get most of the clean boundaries of microservices without the network and operations overhead, and can split a module out later. Example: one app with separate billing, catalog and user modules.
entries.summary: Modular Monolith — A single deployable application divided into strict modules that communicate only through clear interfaces. You get most of the clean boundaries of microservices without the network and operations overhead, and can split a module out later. Example: one app with separate billing, catalog and user…

entries.question: What is Serverless?
entries.answer: **Serverless** — Running code without managing servers — the cloud provider starts it on demand, scales it and bills per request or millisecond. Great for spiky or event-driven work, but has cold starts and time limits. Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions.
entries.summary: Serverless — Running code without managing servers — the cloud provider starts it on demand, scales it and bills per request or millisecond. Great for spiky or event-driven work, but has cold starts and time limits. Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions.

entries.question: What is Event-Driven Architecture?
entries.answer: **Event-Driven Architecture** — A design where services announce events ("OrderPlaced") and other services react to them, instead of calling each other directly. It decouples services and handles spikes well, but makes flows harder to trace. Example: OrderPlaced → payment, email and inventory services each react on their own.
entries.summary: Event-Driven Architecture — A design where services announce events ("OrderPlaced") and other services react to them, instead of calling each other directly. It decouples services and handles spikes well, but makes flows harder to trace. Example: OrderPlaced → payment, email and inventory services each react on their…

entries.question: What is Message Queue / Broker?
entries.answer: **Message Queue / Broker** — A middleman that stores messages from producers until consumers process them, so services can work asynchronously. It smooths traffic spikes and survives a consumer being down. Examples: RabbitMQ (task queues), Kafka (event streams), AWS SQS.
entries.summary: Message Queue / Broker — A middleman that stores messages from producers until consumers process them, so services can work asynchronously. It smooths traffic spikes and survives a consumer being down. Examples: RabbitMQ (task queues), Kafka (event streams), AWS SQS.

entries.question: What is API Gateway?
entries.answer: **API Gateway** — A single entry point in front of many backend services that routes each request and handles shared concerns: authentication, rate limiting, logging and SSL. Clients call one URL instead of many services. Examples: Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway.
entries.summary: API Gateway — A single entry point in front of many backend services that routes each request and handles shared concerns: authentication, rate limiting, logging and SSL. Clients call one URL instead of many services. Examples: Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway.

entries.question: What is Load Balancer?
entries.answer: **Load Balancer** — A component that spreads incoming traffic across several servers so none is overloaded, and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones. It enables both scaling and high availability. Examples: AWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy.
entries.summary: Load Balancer — A component that spreads incoming traffic across several servers so none is overloaded, and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones. It enables both scaling and high availability. Examples: AWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy.

entries.question: What is Caching?
entries.answer: **Caching** — Keeping frequently used data in fast storage (memory) so later requests don't have to hit the slow source again. It cuts latency and database load, but cached data can go stale, so it needs expiry rules. Example: storing product details in Redis for 10 minutes.
entries.summary: Caching — Keeping frequently used data in fast storage (memory) so later requests don't have to hit the slow source again. It cuts latency and database load, but cached data can go stale, so it needs expiry rules. Example: storing product details in Redis for 10 minutes.

entries.question: What is CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
entries.answer: **CDN** (Content Delivery Network) — A network of servers around the world that keeps copies of static content (images, JS, CSS, videos) close to users. Pages load faster and the origin server gets less traffic. Examples: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Akamai.
entries.summary: CDN (Content Delivery Network) — A network of servers around the world that keeps copies of static content (images, JS, CSS, videos) close to users. Pages load faster and the origin server gets less traffic. Examples: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Akamai.

entries.question: What is Scalability (Horizontal / Vertical)?
entries.answer: **Scalability (Horizontal / Vertical)** — A system's ability to handle more load. Vertical scaling uses a bigger machine (more CPU/RAM) — simple but limited; horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer — needs stateless apps but grows much further. Example: going from 2 to 10 app servers during a sale.
entries.summary: Scalability (Horizontal / Vertical) — A system's ability to handle more load. Vertical scaling uses a bigger machine (more CPU/RAM) — simple but limited; horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer — needs stateless apps but grows much further. Example: going from 2 to 10 app servers during a sale.

entries.question: What is High Availability (HA)?
entries.answer: **High Availability (HA)** — Designing a system to stay up even when parts fail, by removing single points of failure with redundancy. It is measured in uptime: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes. Example: running servers in two availability zones with automatic failover.
entries.summary: High Availability (HA) — Designing a system to stay up even when parts fail, by removing single points of failure with redundancy. It is measured in uptime: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes. Example: running servers in two availability zones with automatic failover.

entries.question: What is Fault Tolerance / Resilience?
entries.answer: **Fault Tolerance / Resilience** — The ability to keep working, perhaps in a reduced way, when some parts fail. Techniques include timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks and redundancy. Example: if the recommendation service is down, the shop page still loads without recommendations.
entries.summary: Fault Tolerance / Resilience — The ability to keep working, perhaps in a reduced way, when some parts fail. Techniques include timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks and redundancy. Example: if the recommendation service is down, the shop page still loads without recommendations.

entries.question: What is Circuit Breaker?
entries.answer: **Circuit Breaker** — A pattern that stops calling a failing service for a while after repeated errors, returning a fallback instead. This prevents threads piling up and failures spreading; after a pause it lets a few test calls through. Example: Resilience4j opens the circuit after 50% of calls to the payment API fail.
entries.summary: Circuit Breaker — A pattern that stops calling a failing service for a while after repeated errors, returning a fallback instead. entries.question: What is CAP Theorem?
entries.answer: **CAP Theorem** — In a distributed system, when the network splits (a partition), you must choose between consistency (everyone sees the same latest data) and availability (every request gets an answer). Partitions can't be avoided, so the real choice is C or A during one. Example: a bank balance favours consistency; a social feed favours availability.

entries.question: What is Saga Pattern?
entries.answer: **Saga Pattern** — A way to keep data consistent across microservices without one big transaction: each service does its local step, and if a later step fails, earlier steps are undone with compensating actions. Example: order created → payment taken → stock fails → refund payment and cancel order.
entries.summary: Saga Pattern — A way to keep data consistent across microservices without one big transaction: each service does its local step, and if a later step fails, earlier steps are undone with compensating actions. Example: order created → payment taken → stock fails → refund payment and cancel order.

entries.question: What is CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)?
entries.answer: **CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) — Using separate models (and often separate databases) for writes (commands) and reads (queries). Each side can be optimised and scaled on its own, at the cost of extra complexity and slightly delayed reads. Example: orders are written to PostgreSQL and copied to Elasticsearch for fast search.

entries.question: What is DDD (Domain-Driven Design)?
entries.answer: **DDD** (Domain-Driven Design) — An approach that designs software around the business domain, using the same language as business experts. It splits a large system into bounded contexts, each with its own model. Example: 'customer' means different things in Billing and Shipping, so each context has its own Customer model.
entries.summary: DDD (Domain-Driven Design) — An approach that designs software around the business domain, using the same language as business experts. It splits a large system into bounded contexts, each with its own model. Example: 'customer' means different things in Billing and Shipping, so each context has its own Customer model.

entries.question: What is Hexagonal / Clean Architecture?
entries.answer: **Hexagonal / Clean Architecture** — Architectures that keep core business logic at the centre, independent of frameworks, UI and databases, which plug in through interfaces (ports and adapters). This makes the core easy to test and technology easy to swap. Example: switching MySQL to MongoDB changes only an adapter, not the business rules.

entries.question: What is Service Mesh?
entries.answer: **Service Mesh** — An infrastructure layer, usually sidecar proxies next to each service, that handles service-to-service traffic: encryption (mTLS), retries, routing and metrics — without changing application code. Useful when you run many microservices. Examples: Istio, Linkerd.
entries.summary: Service Mesh — An infrastructure layer, usually sidecar proxies next to each service, that handles service-to-service traffic: encryption (mTLS), retries, routing and metrics — without changing application code. Useful when you run many microservices. Examples: Istio, Linkerd.

entries.question: What is Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)?
entries.answer: **Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)** — Requirements about how well the system works rather than what it does: performance, scalability, availability, security, usability, maintainability. They drive architecture choices and must be measurable. Example: 'search must respond in under 300 ms for 5,000 concurrent users'.
entries.summary: Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) — Requirements about how well the system works rather than what it does: performance, scalability, availability, security, usability, maintainability. entries.question: What is ADR (Architecture Decision Record)?
entries.answer: **ADR** (Architecture Decision Record) — A short document that records one important architecture decision: the context, the options considered, the choice and its consequences. It tells future team members why things are the way they are. Example: 'ADR-007: Use Kafka instead of RabbitMQ for order events because we need replay'.
entries.summary: ADR (Architecture Decision Record) — A short document that records one important architecture decision: the context, the options considered, the choice and its consequences.
